  • Intuitionistic logic, dual intuitionistic logic, and modality
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We explore various semantic understandings of dual intuitionistic logic by exploring the relationship between co-Heyting algebras and topological spaces. First, we discuss the relevant ideas in the setting of Heyting algebras and intuitionistic logic, showing organically the progression from the primordial example of lattices of open sets of topological spaces to more general ways of thinking about Heyting algebras. Then, we adapt the ideas to the dual intuitionistic setting, and use them to prove a number of interesting properties, including a deep relationship both intuitionistic and dual intuitionistic logic share through Kripke semantics to the modal logic $\mathsf{S4}$.

  • join of categories in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The excerpt defines the join of two categories \(C\) and \(C'\) as a category with objects formed by the disjoint union of \(C\) and \(C'\), and morphisms including all original morphisms plus a unique morphism from every object of \(C\) to every object of \(C'\). This construction is described equivalently as the cograph of a unique profunctor mapping all object pairs to the terminal set. The text demonstrates that the join arises naturally as a right adjoint to a specific functor induced by the inclusion of the boundary of the standard 1-simplex, establishing a bijection between functors from the join to a pair of categories and functors from the individual categories to the target categories. It further characterizes the join as a directed or lopsided coproduct, distinguishing it from the standard coproduct by its weighting, and notes its relationship to the cocomma of a product cone.

  • k & \text{if }
    people.math.harvard.eduPDF documentsFirst four PDF pages
    Summary

    This excerpt presents Jacob Lurie's expository account of the classification of topological field theories, specifically addressing a version of the cobordism hypothesis conjectured by Baez and Dolan. The work defines an n-dimensional topological field theory as a symmetric monoidal functor from the category of closed oriented (n-1)-manifolds and bordisms to vector spaces, introducing extended theories to handle higher-dimensional generalizations via higher category theory. The text aims to refine Atiyah's classical definition by accounting for the homotopy types of diffeomorphism groups. It details how a functor Z assigns scalars to closed manifolds and explains that bordisms like M × [0, 1] represent identity, evaluation, and coevaluation maps. Proposition 1.1.8 asserts that for any closed (n-1)-manifold M, the associated vector space Z(M) is finite-dimensional and the induced pairing is perfect, establishing an isomorphism between Z(M) and its dual. The author explicitly notes this is an informal account omitting precise definitions and proofs, with a more detailed treatment reserved for future publication.

  • Kan extension in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Kan extensions represent a fundamental concept in category theory that generalizes adjoint functors, limits, and colimits by providing the best approximation for extending a functor or lifting a morphism across various categorical structures, including 2-categories and n-categories. The approach distinguishes between global and local variants, ordinary and weak types, and pointwise versus absolute extensions, with pointwise constructions relying on weighted (co)limits when the codomain admits sufficient structure. In enriched settings, these reduce to ordinary conical limits over comma categories, while absolute extensions are universally preserved by all functors. Practical existence is often secured through size constraints like the sharp and tame Kan lemmas, and the theory demonstrates ubiquity by subsuming representable functors and modeling operations such as sheaf-theoretic pullbacks and push-forwards in physics. While powerful, the equipment-theoretic approach is sometimes necessary in general 2-categories where standard comma objects fail to capture 2-cells, and the existence of global extensions may not always be guaranteed even if local ones are defined.

  • Kleisli object in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    This source defines Kleisli objects within 2-categories as universal right modules for a given monad, characterizing them via a free 1-morphism and a 2-morphism that induce a natural isomorphism between hom-sets and module categories. It establishes that these objects generalize ordinary Kleisli categories from the 2-category of categories and functions, extending to bicategories of relations and profunctors where they facilitate factorizations of functors. The text further demonstrates formal dualities, noting that Kleisli objects correspond to Eilenberg-Moore objects in the opposite 2-category and represent specific weighted 2-colimits, while referencing a 2016 Advances in Mathematics article for the generalization of these concepts to categories enriched in a bicategory, termed "collages."

  • Locale Basics
    grossack.siteOther websites
    Summary

    The source synthesizes foundational concepts of locale theory, defining locales as the opposite category of frames—lattices closed under arbitrary joins satisfying the distributive law—and explores their construction from geometric objects like real numbers and circles. It introduces flat sites to manage metric spaces where basic opens lack closed intersections and defines the frame presented by such sites. The text establishes a logical dual through geometric theories, using formulas and sequents to construct the Lindenbaum algebra as a classifying locale that models theories via frame homomorphisms. It clarifies that points correspond to continuous maps from the terminal locale and asserts every locale arises as a classifying locale for a specific geometric theory. Furthermore, the excerpt highlights that locales function as the free cocompletion of a category, behave more robustly than topological spaces under constructive interpretations, and extend theorems to bundles of locales via slice category equivalences, while referencing Johnstone's *Stone Spaces* and Vickers' work on stability axioms.

  • logical functor in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    A logical morphism between elementary toposes is a homomorphism that preserves all elementary topos structure, specifically finite limits and power objects, thereby maintaining the context for first-order logic without necessarily preserving infinitary structures found in sheaf toposes. Formally defined by the preservation of finite limits and the isomorphism of the canonical morphism relating power objects, such functors are locally cartesian closed and Heyting functors. While distinct from geometric morphisms which preserve sheaf topos structure, logical functors can be combined with geometric morphisms to form atomic geometric morphisms when the inverse image is logical. Key properties include the existence of a right adjoint under specific conditions, the preservation of subobject relationships, and the ability to reflect truth in internal logic if conservative. Examples include inclusions of finite sets into sets and forgetful functors from group representations, illustrating their role in categorifying Heyting algebra homomorphisms and enabling principles like those in nonstandard analysis.

  • Mathematical Foundations for a Compositional Account of the Bayesian Brain
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    This dissertation reports some first steps towards a compositional account of active inference and the Bayesian brain. Specifically, we use the tools of contemporary applied category theory to supply functorial semantics for approximate inference. To do so, we define on the `syntactic' side the new notion of Bayesian lens and show that Bayesian updating composes according to the compositional lens pattern. Using Bayesian lenses, and inspired by compositional game theory, we define fibrations of statistical games and classify various problems of statistical inference as corresponding sections: the chain rule of the relative entropy is formalized as a strict section, while maximum likelihood estimation and the free energy give lax sections. In the process, we introduce a new notion of `copy-composition'. On the `semantic' side, we present a new formalization of general open dynamical systems (particularly: deterministic, stochastic, and random; and discrete- and continuous-time) as certain coalgebras of polynomial functors, which we show collect into monoidal opindexed categories (or, alternatively, into algebras for multicategories of generalized polynomial functors). We use these opindexed categories to define monoidal bicategories of cilia: dynamical systems which control lenses, and which supply the target for our functorial semantics. Accordingly, we construct functors which explain the bidirectional compositional structure of predictive coding neural circuits under the free energy principle, thereby giving a formal mathematical underpinning to the bidirectionality observed in the cortex. Along the way, we explain how to compose rate-coded neural circuits using an algebra for a multicategory of linear circuit diagrams, showing subsequently that this is subsumed by lenses and polynomial functors.

  • Maths in Lean: category theory
    leanprover-community.github.ioOther websites
    Summary

    This source excerpt details the Lean Mathlib library's structure for category theory, specifying that the Category typeclass resides in Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Category.Basic and relies on object types for inference. It locates Functors in Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Functor.Basic, Natural transformations in Mathlib.CategoryTheory.NatTrans, and the category of functors in Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Functor.Category. The text defines specific notations for morphisms using the ⟶ arrow, identity morphisms with 𝟙, and composition via ≫, while also offering a local definition for the alternative ⊚ notation. Isomorphisms are denoted by ≅, and functors are represented by ⥤ with actions on objects and morphisms accessed via F.obj and F.map respectively. Natural transformations use τ.app for components and F ⟶ G for types, supporting both vertical composition with ≫ and horizontal composition with hcomp.

  • Matteo Capucci in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Matteo Capucci is a PhD candidate at the University of Strathclyde, advised by Neil Ghani, who applies categorical ideas to systems theory, particularly cybernetics, while exploring the intersection of quantitative and structural methods. His research includes foundational work on categorical cybernetics published in EPTCS 372 (2022) and the diegetic representation of feedback in open games in EPTCS 380 (2023). He investigates external choice in game theory as a quasi-limit and develops higher category theoretic generalizations of the para construction for dynamical systems. Additionally, he constructs triple categories of cybernetic processes and presents the para construction as a wreath product at the CQTS conference in January 2024. His interests also extend to quantitative first-order logic and the dependently-typed generalization of optics, though specific details on these latter topics remain listed as areas of interest without further elaboration in the provided text.

  • measurable locale in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Measurable locales, a concept introduced by Dmitri Pavlov, serve as a foundation for measure theory analogous to how general locales underpin topology, particularly in constructive mathematics. Defined equivalently via compact strictly localizable measure spaces, commutative von Neumann algebras, or continuous valuations, these structures form the category Meas Loc, which is a full subcategory of the category of complete Boolean algebras. While classically defined through isomorphisms to Boolean algebras of measurable sets modulo null sets, constructive definitions often rely on W*-algebras to avoid requiring decidable equality. Morphisms in this category correspond to continuous maps preserving joins, and the theory includes specific examples such as the empty space, the two-element Boolean algebra, and the real line as Lebesgue-measurable sets modulo null sets. A key result establishes that every measurable locale is dually a direct product of copies of the two-element algebra, though this classification may not hold constructively. The framework supports the construction of Borel measurable locales from any locale via representable functors and facilitates the definition of normal measures, which are essential for developing measure theory in this context.

  • Memory Evolutive Systems; Hierarchy, Emergence, Cognition
    shop.elsevier.comOther websites
    Summary

    Memory Evolutive Systems; Hierarchy, Emergence, Cognition provides comprehensive and comprehensible coverage of Memory Evolutive Systems (MEM). Written by the developers of the MEM, the book proposes a mathematical model for autonomous evolutionary systems based on the Category Theory of mathematics. It describes a framework to study and possibly simulate the structure of living systems and their dynamic behavior. This book contributes to understanding the multidisciplinary interfaces between mathematics, cognition, consciousness, biology and the study of complexity. It is organized into three parts. Part A deals with hierarchy and emergence and covers such topics as net of interactions and categories; the binding problem; and complexifications and emergence. Part B is about MEM while Part C discusses MEM applications to cognition and consciousness. The book explores the characteristics of a complex evolutionary system, its differences from inanimate physical systems, and its functioning and evolution in time, from its birth to its death. This book is an ideal reference for researchers, teachers and students in pure mathematics, computer science, cognitive science, study of complexity and systems theory, Category Theory, biological systems theory, and consciousness theory. It would also be of interest to both individuals and institutional libraries.

  • microcosm principle in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The microcosm principle posits that algebraic structures can be defined internally within categories equipped with a categorified version of the same structure, such as monoid objects in monoidal categories. While initially a heuristic, formal definitions exist for various contexts: Baez and Dolan defined internal algebras via lax morphisms from terminal objects in higher categorical settings, Batanin extended this to cartesian monads and internal categories, and Hasuo, Jacobs, and Sokolova applied it to Lawvere theories to prove results on lifting structures to coalgebras. In higher algebra and homotopy theory, Jacob Lurie provided a rigorous framework where an algebra over an operad in an $(\infty,1)$-category is equivalently encoded by a coCartesian fibration of operads, with the algebra corresponding to a section of this map. These formalizations demonstrate how internal algebraic structures generalize standard notions across different levels of categorification.

  • Modeling Hierarchical System with Operads
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    This paper applies operads and functorial semantics to address the problem of failure diagnosis in complex systems. We start with a concrete example, developing a hierarchical interaction model for the Length Scale Interferometer, a high-precision measurement system operated by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. The model is expressed in terms of combinatorial/diagrammatic structures called port-graphs, and we explain how to extract an operad LSI from a collection of these diagrams. Next we show how functors to the operad of probabilities organize and constrain the relative probabilities of component failure in the system. Finally, we show how to extend the analysis from general component failure to specific failure modes.

  • Obstructions to Compositionality
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Compositionality is at the heart of computer science and several other areas of applied category theory such as computational linguistics, categorical quantum mechanics, interpretable AI, dynamical systems, compositional game theory, and Petri nets. However, the meaning of the term seems to vary across the many different applications. This work contributes to understanding, and in particular qualifying, different kinds of compositionality. Formally, we introduce invariants of categories that we call zeroth and first homotopy posets, generalising in a precise sense the pi0 and pi1 of a groupoid. These posets can be used to obtain a qualitative description of how far an object is from being terminal and a morphism is from being iso. In the context of applied category theory, this formal machinery gives us a way to qualitatively describe the "failures of compositionality", seen as failures of certain (op)lax functors to be strong, by classifying obstructions to the (op)laxators being isomorphisms. Failure of compositionality, for example for the interpretation of a categorical syntax in a semantic universe, can both be a bad thing and a good thing, which we illustrate by respective examples in graph theory and quantum theory.

  • On (Enriched) Left Bousfield Localization of Model Categories
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    I verify the existence of left Bousfield localizations and of enriched left Bousfield localizations, and I prove a collection of useful technical results characterizing certain fibrations of (enriched) left Bousfield localizations. I also use such Bousfield localizations to construct a number of new model categories, including models for the homotopy limit of right Quillen presheaves, for Postnikov towers in model categories, and for presheaves valued in a symmetric monoidal model category satisfying a homotopy-coherent descent condition.

  • On enriched terms and 2-categorical universal algebra
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We introduce a new notion of recursively generated enriched term which generalizes the one studied in joint work with Rosick\'y. These new terms come together with a notion of term-interpretability, which recovers the same type of interpretability that has been considered for enrichment over posets, metric spaces, and $\omega$-complete posets. As an application of this, we specialize to the 2-categorical case by considering 2-dimensional terms and 2-dimensional equational theories. In this context we also give an explicit description of free structures and prove a 2-dimensional Birkhoff variety theorem.

  • On the Classification of Topological Field Theories
    arxiv.orgResearch papersAccessible page excerpt
    Summary

    This expository draft outlines a proof of a version of the Baez-Dolan cobordism hypothesis conjecture, aiming to classify topological field theories using higher category theory. The text defines an $n$-dimensional topological field theory as a symmetric monoidal functor from the category of closed oriented $(n-1)$-manifolds and bordisms to vector spaces, establishing that in low dimensions, such theories are determined by algebraic structures like Frobenius algebras. While the author demonstrates how invariants are computed by decomposing manifolds, the excerpt explicitly notes that the paper provides only an informal account without precise definitions or careful proofs, reserving detailed accounts for future work. A key contribution is the proposal to extend these theories to higher dimensions by incorporating data for manifolds of lower dimensions, formalized within the language of weak $2$-categories to accommodate the difficulties of defining strictly associative composition laws in higher dimensions. The approach relies on weak $n$-categories because strict $n$-categories for $n>2$ are described as poorly behaved, though the text acknowledges the complexity introduced by requiring coherent isomorphisms rather than exact associativity.

  • Operads and Phylogenetic Trees
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We construct an operad $\mathrm{Phyl}$ whose operations are the edge-labelled trees used in phylogenetics. This operad is the coproduct of $\mathrm{Com}$, the operad for commutative semigroups, and $[0,\infty)$, the operad with unary operations corresponding to nonnegative real numbers, where composition is addition. We show that there is a homeomorphism between the space of $n$-ary operations of $\mathrm{Phyl}$ and $\mathcal{T}_n\times [0,\infty)^{n+1}$, where $\mathcal{T}_n$ is the space of metric $n$-trees introduced by Billera, Holmes and Vogtmann. Furthermore, we show that the Markov models used to reconstruct phylogenetic trees from genome data give coalgebras of $\mathrm{Phyl}$. These always extend to coalgebras of the larger operad $\mathrm{Com} + [0,\infty]$, since Markov processes on finite sets converge to an equilibrium as time approaches infinity. We show that for any operad $O$, its coproduct with $[0,\infty]$ contains the operad $W(O)$ constucted by Boardman and Vogt. To prove these results, we explicitly describe the coproduct of operads in terms of labelled trees.

  • periodic table in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    This source excerpt discusses periodic tables in higher category theory, homotopy theory, and homotopy type theory, drawing an analogy to Mendeleev's chemical table to predict undiscovered mathematical structures like n-categories and n-truncated types. It details the first such table by John Baez and James Dolan, which classifies k-tuply monoidal n-categories across rows indexed by k and columns by n, ranging from trivial structures to symmetric monoidal categories. The text notes that while the original table focused on k-tuply monoidal n-categories, subsequent analysis by Eugenia Cheng and Nick Gurski suggests the table behaves more correctly when restricted to (k-1)-simply connected (n+k)-categories or when examining the 'pointed' version. These tables serve as organizational tools that inspire the invention of new varieties of higher algebraic objects, functioning similarly to how chemical periodic tables predicted undiscovered elements.

  • Poly: An abundant categorical setting for mode-dependent dynamics
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Dynamical systems---by which we mean machines that take time-varying input, change their state, and produce output---can be wired together to form more complex systems. Previous work has shown how to allow collections of machines to reconfigure their wiring diagram dynamically, based on their collective state. This notion was called "mode dependence", and while the framework was compositional (forming an operad of re-wiring diagrams and algebra of mode-dependent dynamical systems on it), the formulation itself was more "creative" than it was natural. In this paper we show that the theory of mode-dependent dynamical systems can be more naturally recast within the category Poly of polynomial functors. This category is almost superlatively abundant in its structure: for example, it has \emph{four} interacting monoidal structures $(+,\times,\otimes,\circ)$, two of which ($\times,\otimes$) are monoidal closed, and the comonoids for $\circ$ are precisely categories in the usual sense. We discuss how the various structures in Poly show up in the theory of dynamical systems. We also show that the usual coalgebraic formalism for dynamical systems takes place within Poly. Indeed one can see coalgebras as special dynamical systems---ones that do not record their history---formally analogous to contractible groupoids as special categories.

  • Programs as Singularities
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We develop a correspondence between the structure of Turing machines and the structure of singularities of real analytic functions, based on connecting the Ehrhard-Regnier derivative from linear logic with the role of geometry in Watanabe's singular learning theory. The correspondence works by embedding ordinary (discrete) Turing machine codes into a family of noisy codes which form a smooth parameter space. On this parameter space we consider a potential function which has Turing machines as critical points. By relating the Taylor series expansion of this potential at such a critical point to combinatorics of error syndromes, we relate the local geometry to internal structure of the Turing machine. The potential in question is the negative log-likelihood for a statistical model, so that the structure of the Turing machine and its associated singularity is further related to Bayesian inference. Two algorithms that produce the same predictive function can nonetheless correspond to singularities with different geometries, which implies that the Bayesian posterior can discriminate between distinct algorithmic implementations, contrary to a purely functional view of inference. In the context of singular learning theory our results point to a more nuanced understanding of Occam's razor and the meaning of simplicity in inductive inference.

  • Rank-finiteness - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Rank-finiteness in mathematics concerns whether fusion categories possess a finite or infinite number of equivalence classes for a given rank, defined as the count of simple object isomorphism classes. The foundational Ocneanu rigidity theorem asserts that every fusion ring has finitely many categorifications, relying on the vanishing of Davydov-Yetter cohomology groups to classify deformations. While rank-finiteness is established for modular tensor categories by Bruillard, Ng, Rowell, and Wang, and for braided fusion categories by Jones, Morrison, Nikshych, and Rowell, the general case remains unresolved. It is currently unknown if there are finitely many fusion categories, pivotal fusion categories, or spherical fusion categories of a specific rank, linking this problem to the open question of whether every fusion category admits a pivotal or spherical structure.

  • Reflection principle vs universes
    mathoverflow.netDiscussions and essays
    Summary

    The source text discusses the foundational challenges in category theory regarding the use of Grothendieck universes to avoid set-theoretic paradoxes, noting that while historically significant, their reliance on strongly inaccessible cardinals has faced criticism for introducing axioms beyond ZFC. The author explores whether the reflection principle allows for rewriting major works like Lurie's Higher Topos Theory without these large cardinals by replacing them with carefully chosen smaller cardinals satisfying weaker conditions, such as uncountable cofinality. Although a conservative axiom system involving two such cardinals and a reflection schema can be constructed, the text highlights a specific technical difficulty: proving that unions of sets indexed by a set within the universe remain within that universe requires the indexing function itself to be definable within the same level, which complicates the application of standard arguments. The author concludes that while the reflection principle suggests such a rewrite is theoretically possible, the practical implementation requires significant effort to navigate these subtle set-theoretic constraints, leaving the precise answer to whether HTT can be fully rewritten without universes as an open question requiring further expert analysis.

  • Rosen Fibration Theory
    tetrapharmakon.github.ioPDF documentsSource abstract
    Summary

    Robert Rosen’s foundational work at the interface of mathematical biology and category theory combined unripe mathematical tools with considerable inventive insight. In this paper, we rekindle his programme using the resources offered by contemporary category theory. In any monoidal closed category, we can cast the theory of Rosen’s (M,R)-systems: diagrams A f−→B Φ−→[A, B] interpreted as process–repair pairs (f, Φ). These incoherent (M,R)-systems assemble into a total category carrying a canonical span over C, fibred in the input variable but only displayed in the output variable. Examples arise in vector spaces, quantales, Chu spaces, and combinatorial species under convolution and substitution. Repair becomes polymorphic once the repair map is required to be natural. We compare a hierarchy of naturality conditions, preferring to focus on those where the dependence on A, B is functorial; thus, we organise coherent (M,R)-systems into a profunctor, whose tabulator is the Rosen fibration of the title. Naturality is a severe constraint: in Set, and more generally in every localic topos, coherent (M,R)-systems are trivial. Nontrivial examples require the ambient category to carry isotropy, in a sense measured by a certain object of C, the end R X[X, X], which classifies repair maps and which we call the Bernstein centre. We then formalise Rosen’s metabolic closure. A universal closure point is unique when it exists, and an input object admits such a point for some natural repair family exactly when it is a retract of the monoidal unit; the possible inputs are therefore classified by split idempotent scalars. We extend the theory (both the incoherent and the coherent one) to diagrams A →B →[A, B] → [B, [A, B]] →· · · of arbitrary, even infinite, length. Finally, we analyse Arbib’s correspondence between (M,R)-systems and Mealy automata; we upgrade it to a fibred functor, and observe that metabolic closure translates into a fact of classical representation theory: a system is closed exactly when the initial state of the associated automaton has nontrivial isotropy, and a universal closure point is an element of its stabiliser. A substantial part of the mathematics below has been formalised and machine-checked in the Agda proof assistant. Contents

  • Seeing stacks in the Calculus of Functors
    mathoverflow.netDiscussions and essays
    Summary

    The source defines the nth Weiss topology on a topos T by requiring that a family of maps constitutes a covering if its kth cartesian power remains a covering for all 0 ≤ k ≤ n, establishing that higher topologies contain lower ones. Sheaves in these topologies correspond to n-polynomial functors, with the first Weiss topology nearly coinciding with the ordinary topology except for the exclusion of the empty cover. For any presheaf F, the nth Taylor approximation T_n(F) is defined as the sheafification of F in the nth Weiss topology, forming a canonical tower from T_∞(F) down to T_0(F). This framework recovers manifold calculus when applied to the site of manifolds, enriched manifold calculus for the ∞-site of manifolds as defined by Boavida and Weiss, and homotopy calculus for the site of spaces, provided Čech covers are replaced with hypercovers.

  • Semi-strictification of $(\infty, n)$-categories
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We prove the first equivalence between a weak non-algebraic model and a semi-strict algebraic model of $(\infty, n)$-categories. This takes the form of a natural semi-strictification, whereby a weak $(\infty, n)$-category is embedded into a semi-strict one through an acyclic cofibration, in such a way that weak functors lift to semi-strict functors; this constitutes the derived unit of a Quillen equivalence between weak model categories whose fibrant objects are, respectively, the weak $(\infty, n)$-categories and (up to an acyclic fibration) the semi-strict ones. The semi-strict model has algebraic units and composition of round pasting diagrams, satisfying a strict form of associativity and interchange as in Henry's regular version of Simpson's weak units conjecture; semi-strict functors strictly preserve round composition, but only weakly preserve units. Globular composition operations are obtained from a combination of units and round composition. Since the models satisfy the homotopy hypothesis in the case $n = 0$, this result also exhibits the first semi-strict model of the classical homotopy types that has algebraic units and composition. The constructions are based on the combinatorics of regular directed complexes and are entirely explicit and combinatorial, in the spirit of Mac Lane's strictification of bicategories.

  • Set in nLab

    The source excerpt describes the category of sets, Set, as a foundational structure in mathematics, noting that its definition varies based on foundational assumptions like logic type, impredicativity, and choice principles.   • sheafification in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The sheafification functor universally transforms presheaves on a site \(C\) into sheaves by serving as the left adjoint to the inclusion of sheaves into presheaves, thereby exhibiting the category of sheaves as a reflective subcategory. This construction is grounded in the theory of localizations at a set of morphisms \(W\) satisfying a calculus of fractions, specifically the sieve inclusions for covering families, which are completed under small colimits to form \(\bar W\). For a presheaf \(X\), its sheafification \(L(X)\) is defined via a colimit over these morphisms, yielding a natural isomorphism between the hom-sets of the sheafified object and the original presheaf into any sheaf. While this method applies generally to Set-valued presheaves, sheafification for presheaves with values in other categories, such as groups or modules, requires additional assumptions like those provided by essentially algebraic theories to ensure existence and preserve structural properties.

  • sketch in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The notion of a sketch, formalized by Bastiani and Ehresmann in 1972, provides a diagrammatic approach to algebraic theories using small categories equipped with specified cones and cocones to define limits and colimits. A model of a sketch in a category is a functor preserving these specified limits and colimits, and the category of sketches is well-behaved, being complete, cocomplete, cartesian closed, and possessing a symmetric monoidal closed structure via a tensor product. This tensor product allows for the construction of models of combined theories, such as double categories, though the order of the tensor product generally cannot be swapped unless the specified limits and colimits commute. Sketches generalize Lawvere theories and correspond precisely to accessible and locally presentable categories, offering a categorical semantics for type theory while maintaining a close relationship to category theoretic structures like finite products.

  • Specific notions of forcing from the point of view of category theory
    mathoverflow.netDiscussions and essays
    Summary

    The topos-theoretic approach to forcing interprets a poset $P$ as a category, constructs the presheaf topos on it, and subsequently restricts to the subtopos of double-negation sheaves to recover standard weak forcing. While the initial presheaf topos corresponds to strong forcing operating under intuitionistic logic, the sheaf subtopos yields the widely used weak forcing framework. This theoretical development was pioneered in the early work of Lawvere and Tierney, specifically within Lawvere's 1970 paper

  • Spined categories: generalizing tree-width beyond graphs
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Tree-width is an invaluable tool for computational problems on graphs. But often one would like to compute on other kinds of objects (e.g. decorated graphs or even algebraic structures) where there is no known tree-width analogue. Here we define an abstract analogue of tree-width which provides a uniform definition of various tree-width-like invariants including graph tree-width, hypergraph tree-width, complemented tree-width and even new constructions such as the tree-width of modular quotients. We obtain this generalization by developing a general theory of categories that admit abstract analogues of both tree decompositions and tree-width; we call these pseudo-chordal completions and the triangulation functor respectively.

  • stack in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The term stack serves as a traditional synonym for a 2-sheaf or (2,1)-sheaf, functioning as a specific instance within a broader hierarchy of higher categorical generalizations of sheaves. A 1-stack on a site is defined as a pseudo-functor from the opposite category to Cat satisfying descent for all covers, and when valued in the subcategory of groupoids, it is commonly referred to as a stack of groupoids. This concept is closely related to generalized groupoids, with algebraic and differentiable stacks representing specialized cases over sites of schemes or manifolds. The text notes that stacks are often more familiar than sheaves in certain fields, such as Lie theory and orbifold studies. Provisional material by Todd Trimble outlines a categorification of descent data using bicategorical language, where the stack condition requires a canonical functor to be an equivalence for all covering sieves. The concept originates in Jean Giraud's work on non-abelian cohomology and has been further developed in contexts involving classifying toposes and Grothendieck fibrations.

  • String Diagrams with Factorized Densities
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    A growing body of research on probabilistic programs and causal models has highlighted the need to reason compositionally about model classes that extend directed graphical models. Both probabilistic programs and causal models define a joint probability density over a set of random variables, and exhibit sparse structure that can be used to reason about causation and conditional independence. This work builds on recent work on Markov categories of probabilistic mappings to define a category whose morphisms combine a joint density, factorized over each sample space, with a deterministic mapping from samples to return values. This is a step towards closing the gap between recent category-theoretic descriptions of probability measures, and the operational definitions of factorized densities that are commonly employed in probabilistic programming and causal inference.

  • Structured Active Inference (Extended Abstract)
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We introduce structured active inference, a large generalization and formalization of active inference using the tools of categorical systems theory. We cast generative models formally as systems "on an interface", with the latter being a compositional abstraction of the usual notion of Markov blanket; agents are then 'controllers' for their generative models, formally dual to them. This opens the active inference landscape to new horizons, such as: agents with structured interfaces (e.g. with 'mode-dependence', or that interact with computer APIs); agents that can manage other agents; and 'meta-agents', that use active inference to change their (internal or external) structure. With structured interfaces, we also gain structured ('typed') policies, which are amenable to formal verification, an important step towards safe artificial agents. Moreover, we can make use of categorical logic to describe express agents' goals as formal predicates, whose satisfaction may be dependent on the interaction context. This points towards powerful compositional tools to constrain and control self-organizing ensembles of agents.

  • tetracategories
    math.ucr.eduAcademic resources

    The author reflects on their 1994-1995 attempt to define weak n-categories using a visual approach based on polyhedral diagrams, specifically associahedra and monoidahedra, which were intended to represent higher associativity and unit conditions. Although the project faced technical difficulties regarding the interpretation of pasting schemes within local hom-categories, the underlying methods proved effective in dimensions 2 and 3, yielding classical bicategories and tricategories without modification. The work emphasizes the connection between these geometric structures and operads, particularly Stasheff's associahedra, and relies on parity complex structures and bar constructions to formalize the combinatorics. The author notes that while the resulting diagrams are complex, they are generated by a simple machine and provides annotated examples of unit and associativity coherence equations in tetracategorical data, suggesting the approach remains valuable for understanding coherence aspects of higher category theory despite its initial stagnation.

  • The n-Category Café
    golem.ph.utexas.eduAcademic resources
    Summary

    This research generalizes category theory by developing Yoneda structures within a general 2-category, utilizing natural 2-categorical language to replace the complex machinery of enriched category theory. The author defines a Yoneda structure through three specific axioms: the existence of left extensions for admissible objects, the property that these extensions function as absolute left liftings, and a representability condition ensuring specific 2-cells are isomorphisms. To address size issues, the framework introduces 'admissible' objects and arrows, allowing for the formal development of fundamental concepts such as adjunctions, weighted colimits, and the Eilenberg-Moore category. A key contribution is the introduction of 'totality,' which enables a strong adjoint functor theorem by admitting a left adjoint to the Yoneda arrow. While the formalism successfully captures core categorical concepts across diverse contexts like internal categories and enriched categories, the third axiom is identified as too strong for general enriched category theory, representing a primary limitation of the proposed framework.

  • The n-Category Café
    golem.ph.utexas.eduAcademic resources
    Summary

    This source proposes a hierarchical framework for higher-order theories, defining n-theories as structures where models of an (n+1)-theory form an n-category, thereby extending Lawvere theories into higher dimensions. The work distinguishes between syntactic presentations based on types and terms, and semantic presentations realized as structured categories within specific doctrines, noting that while the hierarchy holds for finite-product theories, the resulting semantic structures depend heavily on the chosen doctrine. A central contribution is the development of a research program to construct general deductive systems for syntactic 2-theories within 3-theories, aiming to ensure correct semantics and desirable metatheoretic properties like cut-elimination for dependent type theories. The authors outline progress on cumulative 3-theories covering unstructured, simple, and dependent types, while also targeting a framework for classical logic. Although the interaction between adjacent levels could theoretically generalize to higher dimensions, the text suggests that practical human cognition favors encoding these complex structures within lower-dimensional ones, a concept exemplified by homotopy type theory and cohesive type theory with modalities.

  • The n-Category Café
    golem.ph.utexas.eduAcademic resources
    Summary

    This source defines enriched categories by generalizing standard categories where hom-sets are replaced by objects in a base monoidal category, demonstrating that when this category is the vector spaces, the framework naturally models algebraic structures. The text specifically applies this theory to metric spaces by enriching over the monoidal category of extended non-negative real numbers, thereby defining generalized metric spaces that accommodate asymmetric distances, infinite values, and zero distances between distinct points. Within this structure, enriched functors correspond to distance-non-increasing maps, and the theory supports the construction of functor categories and the Yoneda embedding. Furthermore, the excerpt illustrates how the sup-metric on functions represents a symmetrization of an asymmetric generalized metric derived from a discrete domain, which encodes a partial order on compact subsets that the standard Hausdorff metric discards. The author concludes by reflecting on the utility of this perspective in algebraic topology and the preference of mathematicians for categories of vector spaces or abelian groups over the category of sets, highlighting Lawvere's pivotal role in elucidating this view despite the difficulty of standard texts.

  • The Physicalization of Metamathematics and Its Implications for the Foundations of Mathematics
    www.wolframscience.comOther websites

    This research posits that both metamathematics and physics emerge from observers sampling the unique ruliad structure, which represents the entangled limit of all possible computations. The study argues that human-accessible mathematics functions analogously to how physical observers perceive physical space, suggesting that current axiomatic practices are merely convenient approximations rather than reflections of mathematics' ultimate character. Through a physicalized analysis of the bulk limit of traditional axiomatic approaches, the author presents explicit empirical metamathematics regarding formalized mathematics, introducing concepts such as metamathematical motion, inevitable dualities, proof topology, and metamathematical singularities. The work contends that mathematics is derived from the ruliad in a direct Platonic fashion, implying that only specific axiom collections remain consistent with the inherent constraints of human mathematical observers, while also exploring the historical, philosophical, and foundational implications for the future trajectory of mathematical inquiry.

  • Towards A More Reasonable Semantic Web
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We aim to accelerate the original vision of the semantic web by revisiting design decisions that have defined the semantic web up until now. We propose a shift in direction that more broadly embraces existing data infrastructure by reconsidering the semantic web's logical foundations. We argue to shift attention away from description logic, which has so far underpinned the semantic web, to a different fragment of first-order logic. We argue, using examples from the (geo)spatial domain, that by doing so, the semantic web can be approached as a traditional data migration and integration problem at a massive scale. That way, a huge amount of existing tools and theories can be deployed to the semantic web's benefit, and the original vision of ontology as shared abstraction be reinvigorated.

    This paper introduces axioms for an abstract trace on a balanced monoidal category, defining it as a natural family of functions satisfying vanishing, superposing, and yanking axioms. The authors prove a structure theorem stating that every traced monoidal category arises canonically from a full submonoidal category of a tortile (or ribbon) monoidal category, a construction described as a left biadjoint to the forgetful 2-functor. The text notes that symmetric monoidal categories are special cases where twist isomorphisms are identities, and compact closed categories are special tortile monoidal categories. While the trace generalizes concepts like contraction and feedback, the provided excerpt only covers the introduction, definitions, and initial lemmas regarding diagrammatic reasoning, without presenting the full proof of the structure theorem or the specific example mentioned in the abstract.

  • Two-dimensional transducers
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We define a bicategory $\mathbf{2TDX}$ whose 1-cells provide a categorification of transducers, computational devices extending finite-state automata with output capabilities. This bicategory is a mathematically interesting object: its objects are categories $\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\dots$ and its 1-cells $(\mathcal{Q}, t) : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}$ consist of a category $\mathcal{Q}$ of `states', and a profunctor $$ t : \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{Q}^\text{op}\times\mathcal{Q} \times (\mathcal{B}^*)^\text{op} \to \mathbf{Set} $$ where $\mathcal{B}^*$ denotes the free monoidal category over $\mathcal{B}$. Extending $t$ to $\mathcal{A}^*$ in a canonical way, to each `word' $\underline a$ in $\mathcal{A}^*$ one attaches an endoprofunctor over the category $\mathcal{Q}$ of states, enriched over presheaves on $\mathcal{B}^*$. We discuss a number of other characterizations of the hom-category $\mathbf{2TDX}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$; we establish a Kleisli-like universal property for $\mathbf{2TDX}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})$ and explore the connection of $\mathbf{2TDX}$ to other bicategories of computational models, such as Bob Walters' bicategory of `circuits'; it is convenient to regard $\mathbf{2TDX}$ as the loose bicategory of a double category $\mathbb{D}\mathbf{TDX}$: the bicategory (resp., double category) of profunctors is naturally contained in the bicategory (resp., double category) $\mathbf{2TDX}$ (resp., $\mathbb{D}\mathbf{TDX}$); we study the completeness and cocompleteness properties of $\mathbb{D}\mathbf{TDX}$, the existence of companions and conjoints, and we sketch how monads, adjunctions, and other structures/properties that naturally arise from the definition work in $\mathbb{D}\mathbf{TDX}$.

  • Von Neumann Categories
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    In this paper, we introduce the notion of a von Neumann category, as a generalization and categorification of von Neumann algebra. A von Neumann category is a premonoidal category with compatible dagger structure which embeds as a double commutant into a suitable premonoidal category of Hilbert spaces. The notion was inspired by algebraic quantum field theory. In AQFT, one assigns to open regions in Minkowski space a C*-algebra, called the local algebra. The local algebras are patched together to form a global algebra associated to the AQFT. The key relativistic assumption is Einstein Causality, which says that the algebras associated to spacelike separated regions commute in the global algebra. Premonoidal categories provide a natural framework for lifting such structure from algebras to categories. Thus von Neumann categories serve as a basis for extending the abstract quantum mechanics of Abramsky and Coecke to include relativistic effects. In this paper, we focus on the structure of von Neumann categories. After giving the basic definitions and examples, we consider constructions typically associated to von Neumann algebras, and examine their extensions to the category setting. In particular, we present a crossed product construction for *-premonoidal categories.

It connects these structures to KZ doctrines, showing that locally fully-faithful doctrines define proto-Yoneda structures, and extends the framework to enriched categories and 2-topos theory. The approach relies on viewing the Yoneda embedding into presheaf categories as a tool to classify two-sided discrete fibrations and higher-dimensional analogues of topos theory.   • 14 GEOMETRY AND HIGHER CATEGORY THEORY
    people.mpim-bonn.mpg.dePDF documents
    Summary

    This research establishes a formalism for dualizable presentable stable categories within higher algebra and geometry, resolving foundational size issues by fixing a regular cardinal to define manageable categories of presentable objects. The core contribution is the development of a six-functor formalism utilizing Stefanich rings, which generalize classical algebraic structures to higher categorical levels involving Gestalten, thereby enabling a conservative transition from algebraic geometry to a new geometric theory. This framework successfully handles non-affine loci in rigid-analytic geometry and extends classical duality theories, such as Cartier and Mukai duality, to higher settings where internal Hom functors are representable by n-affine Gestalten without finiteness hypotheses. By characterizing morphisms through properties like n-affineness, n-primeness, and n-suaveness, the study proves that these structures are local with respect to the tautological topology and admit well-behaved adjoints commuting with base change. While the work provides rigorous proofs for specific cases like the motivic Fourier transform and the classification of multiplicative groups, it relies on several conjectures regarding the moduli space of multiplicative monoid stacks and the surjectivity of maps from nonarchimedean motives, indicating that the full extension to general ring stacks remains a proposed direction requiring further verification.

  • A metric on $S^2 \times S^2$ with positive sectional curvature
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We construct a metric on $S^2 \times S^2$ with positive sectional curvature. Starting from the standard metric on $S^2 \times S^2$, we first perform a Cheeger deformation. The resulting metric has nonnegative sectional curvature. We refer to it as a Cheeger-M\"uter metric. We then consider a suitable third order perturbation of this Cheeger-M\"uter metric and show that the perturbed metrics have positive sectional curvature. The proof requires various calculations, some of which have been carried out with the help of MATHEMATICA. The MATHEMATICA code is attached to this submission.

  • A note on the smash product and regular associativity
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    This note is about the smash product of pointed topological spaces, without relying on some convenient subcategory. We deal with its partial associativity properties and their connection with the function spaces, introducing a property of regular associativity related to the colax monoidal structure of the product. We also study a large class of triples of pointed spaces where associativity fails. Lax and colax monoidal structures are unusual and interesting, in category theory. Some parts of this note will be obvious to a topologist and others to a categorist, in order to take into account both backgrounds.

  • Abstract Stone Duality
    www.paultaylor.euOther websites
    Summary

    Abstract Stone Duality (ASD) is a research programme treating topological spaces and continuous functions directly, modeled by the category of all sober spaces rather than just locally compact ones. It establishes a categorical duality between topology and algebra, leveraging the analogy between continuous and computable functions to create an inherently computable framework. ASD employs a syntactic approach that generalizes algebraic notation, utilizing a specific space Σ to represent the topology of any space X via continuous maps. This system supports a strong lattice duality where logical connectives correspond to intersections, unions, and infinite unions of open or closed subspaces, avoiding double negations found in intuitionism. Key concepts include overtness, which relates to recursive enumerability, and the Phoa principle, a finitary form of Scott continuity essential for defining extensional correspondences. The theory re-axiomatises topology to justify definitions by description and compactness, with applications ranging from real analysis to programming languages, supported by numerous draft papers and published works on computable topology.

  • Applied & Computational Topology & Geometry
    actgjournal.orgOther websites
    Summary

    The journal "Applied & Computational Topology & Geometry" (ACTG) publishes high-quality research at the intersection of computational mathematics and geometric or topological methods, emphasizing algorithmic and applied aspects of algebraic geometry and topology. It is completely free for both readers and authors, with all publications openly accessible online. ACTG encourages submissions that bridge theoretical foundations with practical applications, making sophisticated mathematical tools accessible to applied researchers. The journal welcomes submissions in areas including computational algebraic topology, computational algebraic geometry, and various applications such as scientific computing, computer vision, materials science, computational biology, signal processing, machine learning, and mathematical physics.

  • Beyond $K$-Theory: Geometry and Holomorphy in Hyperbolic Band Theory
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Topological $K$-theory supplies the decisive stable classification principle for gapped free-fermion phases in Euclidean crystals once symmetry and stabilization are fixed. In hyperbolic band theory, by contrast, it is less decisive for the full band problem: generalized momentum sectors vary through moduli spaces, but passing to ordinary $K$-classes collapses their geometric and holomorphic variation. We distinguish kinematical holomorphy, in which complex geometry organizes the sector spaces, from dynamical holomorphy, in which that geometry informs a Hamiltonian or projector, and formulate the resulting loss as an observable-factorization problem. For a compact hyperbolic surface $X$, we prove nonfactorization in three settings: fibrewise $K^0(X)$, occupied-state $K^0(B)$, and operator-algebraic $K$-theory. The affected quantities include spectra and Higgs spectral curves, the Berry holonomy and the quantum metric, the partially filled Hall response, and the Fermi surface and nodal geometries. We also identify the quantized pairings and local charges retained by topology. Up to an explicit area factor, the Kotani--Sunada bottom-band Hessian is the Hodge inner product on $H^1(X;\mathbb R)$. Together with the integral intersection form, it recovers the homology-marked principally polarized Jacobian and hence, by Torelli and uniformization, the underlying complex and hyperbolic surface, though not a full Teichm\"uller marking. We also separate finite-rank sectors from the thermodynamic bulk. Locally faithful covers reproduce polynomial traces exactly and control continuous spectral observables. In arithmetic congruence towers, analytic observables converge as $O(|G_n|^{-\eta})$ for some $\eta>0$, and $C^s$ observables as $O((\log |G_n|)^{-s})$, while established coherent large-rank limits recover bulk density-of-states moments.

  • Bott periodicity theorem - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Raoul Bott's periodicity theorem establishes that the homotopy groups of the infinite classical groups U, O, and Sp exhibit periodicity with periods of 2, 8, and 8 respectively, a phenomenon rooted in the structure of Clifford algebras and symmetric spaces. While Bott originally defined "stable" in the context of these direct limits of classical groups rather than stable homotopy groups, the theorem provides a foundational insight into the stable homotopy groups of spheres via the J-homomorphism, resolving the Adams conjecture. The proof, initially utilizing Morse theory, demonstrates that the double loop space of the classifying space BU is homotopy equivalent to BU itself, rendering complex topological K-theory 2-fold periodic, whereas real and quaternionic K-theories are 8-fold periodic. This framework simplifies the computation of previously elusive stable homotopy groups by relating them to the cohomology of characteristic classes and the classification of reductive symmetric spaces.

  • Conformal variational discretisation of infinite dimensional Hamiltonian systems with gradient flow dissipation
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Nonconservative evolution problems describe irreversible processes and dissipative effects in a broad variety of phenomena. Such problems are often characterised by a conservative part, which can be modelled as a Hamiltonian term, and a nonconservative part, in the form of gradient flow dissipation. Traditional numerical approximations of this class of problem typically fail to retain the separation into conservative and nonconservative parts hence leading to unphysical solutions. In this work we propose a mixed variational method that gives a semi-discrete problem with the same geometric structure as the infinite-dimensional problem. As a consequence the conservation laws and the dissipative terms are retained. A priori convergence estimates on the solution are established. Numerical tests of the Korteweg-de Vries equation and of the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations on the torus and on the sphere are presented to corroborate the theoretical findings.

  • CW-spectrum in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The CW-spectrum is the sequential spectrum analogue of a CW-complex, serving as a cofibrant object in the stable model structure on topological sequential spectra. Defined by components that are CW-complexes and structure maps which are subcomplex inclusions, a CW-spectrum is constructed as the union of its cells, where a cell is a cell of a component space suspended to all higher degrees under specific non-suspension conditions. Finite and countable spectra are distinguished by the number of constituent cells. The category of CW-spectra, denoted CWSpec, is formed by localizing the category of CW-spectra with levelwise maps at cofinal inclusions, allowing morphisms to be represented by functions from cofinal subspectra. This construction ensures that every sequential spectrum admits a CW-approximation via a stable weak homotopy equivalence, a result supported by the Quillen equivalence between the stable model structure on topological sequential spectra and the stable Bousfield-Friedlander model structure on sequential spectra in simplicial sets.

  • Dagger Categories in Riemannian Geometry
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    A dagger on a category assigns to every morphism $f \colon X \to Y$ a morphism $f^\dagger \colon Y \to X$, contravariantly and involutively, in the way the transpose reverses a real matrix. We show that on the categories of linear algebra and differential geometry, daggers encode metric and Riemannian structures. As is known, on a single vector space, an anti-involution of the endomorphism ring is the adjoint of a form that is determined up to a scalar. But more generally, on the category of all finite-dimensional vector spaces, a dagger is the adjoint for an involution of the scalars together with a unique unimodular Hermitian form on every space. The same holds for finitely generated projective modules over a commutative ring, and hence, through the Serre-Swan correspondence, for vector bundles, where a dagger is a choice of bundle metrics. The dagger structure expresses notions of orthogonality categorically: orthogonal complements and normal bundles acquire universal properties, and Hermitian modules form a dagger compact category. Moreover, daggers on Lie groups, Lie groupoids and their infinitesimal counterparts capture unitary representations and metric connections: a connection is metric precisely when its parallel transport is a dagger functor, or, infinitesimally, when its splitting of the Atiyah sequence commutes with the daggers. Finally, we classify the daggers on the locally graded category of differential operators of a Lie-Rinehart algebra. They correspond to metric-divergence structures, consisting of a real structure, a divergence, and a unimodular Hermitian form on every finitely generated projective module, and they act on operators as formal adjoints; Green's formula expresses the difference between an operator and its adjoint as a divergence.

    Diagrammatic sets are presheaves on a rich category of shapes, whose definition is motivated by combinatorial topology and higher-dimensional diagram rewriting.     ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Discrete Morse theory extends standard Morse theory to finite CW complexes by utilizing simple homotopy theory, specifically through acyclic matchings that partition cells into three disjoint classes with a distinguished bijection. The central result states that if a complex admits an acyclic matching with $n$ critical cells, it is homotopy equivalent to a complex with $n$ cells, achieved via gradient-like paths and collapses rather than flow lines. These paths are defined by alternating sequences of matched cells where multiplicities are calculated using attaching map degrees, ensuring no backward traversal. The resulting Morse complex, constructed from critical cells with a boundary operator summing path multiplicities, yields integer homology groups identical to the original complex. This framework has proven valuable in topological combinatorics for characterizing wedges of spheres, in commutative algebra for minimal resolutions of ideals, and in computational tools like CHomP and Perseus for persistent homology.

  • Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material

    The Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms, introduced by Samuel Eilenberg and Norman Steenrod in 1945, define the common properties of homology theories in algebraic topology, with singular homology being the primary example. These axioms, applied to sequences of functors from topological space pairs to abelian groups, include homotopy, excision, dimension, additivity, and exactness, enabling proofs like the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for all theories satisfying them. Omitting the dimension axiom yields extraordinary homology theories, such as K-theory and cobordism, which emerged in the 1950s. Direct derivations from these axioms confirm that homotopically equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology groups and allow calculations for simple spaces like spheres, supporting proofs of the Brouwer fixed point theorem regarding retracts.

    Alexander Grothendieck's 1984 proposal, "Esquisse d'un Programme," outlined a long-term research plan for the Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, which he held from 1984 to 1988 while maintaining his affiliation with the University of Montpellier. Although the proposal was not formally published until 1997 due to the author's unavailability, its core concepts, including dessins d'enfants and anabelian geometry, have significantly influenced modern mathematics. Anabelian geometry specifically proposes that the algebraic fundamental group of a variety determines its mapping properties when the group is non-abelian. The text notes that while the work remained unpublished for years, it inspired substantial developments in Galois theory, extending it from groups to groupoids and categories, and led to the emergence of the motivic Galois group and Grothendieck topology in the 21st century.

    A fuzzy sphere is a noncommutative geometric variant of an n-sphere, typically the 2-sphere, defined as the formal dual to a specific associative algebra within the matrix algebra \(Mat_{N \times N}\). This algebra is generated by the \(N\)-dimensional complex irreducible representation of the \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) Lie algebra, where the generators satisfy commutation relations that become commutative in the large \(N\) limit, recovering the smooth algebra of the unit 2-sphere. The volume of the fuzzy sphere scales with \(N\) and converges to the standard sphere's volume as \(N\) approaches infinity. While the large \(N\) limit yields a single radius observable, finite \(N\) introduces ordering ambiguities in higher-order functions, where the combinatorics of single trace observables are encoded in chord diagrams and evaluated using \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)-Lie algebra weight systems. These structures appear in D-brane geometry, matrix models like BMN and IKKT, and supersymmetric quantum field theories, extending to higher-dimensional fuzzy spheres such as the 3-sphere and 4-sphere.

The method relies on analyzing the asymptotic expansion of the diagonal heat kernel as time approaches zero, where the constant term must coincide with the local Atiyah-Singer polynomial while negative powers of time vanish.   • Intrinsic Gaussian Vector Fields on Manifolds

    Various applications ranging from robotics to climate science require modeling signals on non-Euclidean domains, such as the sphere. Gaussian process models on manifolds have recently been proposed for such tasks, in particular when uncertainty quantification is needed. In the manifold setting, vector-valued signals can behave very differently from scalar-valued ones, with much of the progress so far focused on modeling the latter. The former, however, are crucial for many applications, such as modeling wind speeds or force fields of unknown dynamical systems. In this paper, we propose novel Gaussian process models for vector-valued signals on manifolds that are intrinsically defined and account for the geometry of the space in consideration. We provide computational primitives needed to deploy the resulting Hodge-Mat\'ern Gaussian vector fields on the two-dimensional sphere and the hypertori. Further, we highlight two generalization directions: discrete two-dimensional meshes and "ideal" manifolds like hyperspheres, Lie groups, and homogeneous spaces. Finally, we show that our Gaussian vector fields constitute considerably more refined inductive biases than the extrinsic fields proposed before.

  • Isospectral - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    In mathematics, isospectral linear operators share the same spectrum, including eigenvalue multiplicities, with behavior differing significantly between finite and infinite dimensions. While finite-dimensional isospectral diagonalizable matrices are similar, infinite-dimensional cases involve the Laplace operator on domains or manifolds, leading to the problem of "hearing the shape of a drum." Fundamental insights in soliton theory link spectral conservation to infinitesimal equations like A' = [A, M]. In spectral geometry, two closed Riemannian manifolds are isospectral if their Laplace–Beltrami operators have coinciding eigenvalues, a concept explored through arithmetic constructions by Milnor and Vignéras using Selberg's trace formula. Toshikazu Sunada later developed a general covering space method based on subgroup properties to generate isospectral but non-isometric manifolds, which enabled the discovery of counterexamples to Kac's conjecture. Despite these advances, simply connected isospectral examples exist that cannot be derived via Sunada's technique, highlighting the complexity of determining geometric properties from spectral data alone.

  • Jets and differential linear logic
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We prove that the category of vector bundles over a fixed smooth manifold and its corresponding category of convenient modules are models for intuitionistic differential linear logic. The exponential modality is modelled by composing the jet comonad, whose Kleisli category has linear differential operators as morphisms, with the more familiar distributional comonad, whose Kleisli category has smooth maps as morphisms. Combining the two comonads gives a new interpretation of the semantics of differential linear logic where the Kleisli morphisms are smooth local functionals, or equivalently, smooth partial differential operators, and the codereliction map induces the functional derivative. This points towards a logic and hence computational theory of non-linear partial differential equations and their solutions based on variational calculus.

  • Organizing Physics with Open Energy-Driven Systems
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Organizing physics has been a long-standing preoccupation of applied category theory, going back at least to Lawvere. We contribute to this research thread by noticing that Hamiltonian mechanics and gradient descent depend crucially on a consistent choice of transformation -- which we call a reaction structure -- from the cotangent bundle to the tangent bundle. We then construct a compositional theory of reaction structures. Reaction-based systems offer a different perspective on composition in physics than port-Hamiltonian systems or open classical mechanics, in that reaction-based composition does not create any new constraints that must be solved for algebraically. The technical contributions of this paper are the development of symmetric monoidal categories of open energy-driven systems and open differential equations, and a functor between them, functioning as a "functorial semantics" for reaction structures. This approach echoes what has previously been done for open games and open gradient-based learners, and in fact subsumes the latter. We then illustrate our theory by constructing an n-fold pendulum as a composite of n-many pendula.

  • Persistent Homology of Coarse Grained State Space Networks

    This work is dedicated to the topological analysis of complex transitional networks for dynamic state detection. Transitional networks are formed from time series data and they leverage graph theory tools to reveal information about the underlying dynamic system. However, traditional tools can fail to summarize the complex topology present in such graphs. In this work, we leverage persistent homology from topological data analysis to study the structure of these networks. We contrast dynamic state detection from time series using a coarse-grained state-space network (CGSSN) and topological data analysis (TDA) to two state of the art approaches: ordinal partition networks (OPNs) combined with TDA and the standard application of persistent homology to the time-delay embedding of the signal. We show that the CGSSN captures rich information about the dynamic state of the underlying dynamical system as evidenced by a significant improvement in dynamic state detection and noise robustness in comparison to OPNs. We also show that because the computational time of CGSSN is not linearly dependent on the signal's length, it is more computationally efficient than applying TDA to the time-delay embedding of the time series.

  • Physical consequences of cobordism hypothesis?

    The text explains that topological field theories (TQFTs) must satisfy a locality axiom, meaning their data and partition functions can be constructed by gluing information from arbitrarily small neighborhoods, effectively reducing the theory to data on Ω₁₂₃ or points rather than full manifolds. This principle underpins the cobordism hypothesis, which posits that a fully extended TQFT is determined by its value on a point, replacing the need for collars found in non-topological quantum field theories. The discussion highlights physical applications in condensed matter physics, where low-energy descriptions of topological phases of matter and symmetry-protected topological phases are conjectured to be fully extended TQFTs and invertible TQFTs, respectively. Specific examples include the classification of 3D topological phases via spherical fusion categories and the classification of SPT phases using Madsen-Tillmann spectra, with recent work by Freed, Hopkins, and others providing strong evidence and proofs for these conjectures.

  • Physics, Topology, Logic and Computation: A Rosetta Stone
