    In physics, Feynman diagrams are used to reason about quantum processes. In the 1980s, it became clear that underlying these diagrams is a powerful analogy between quantum physics and topology: namely, a linear operator behaves very much like a "cobordism". Similar diagrams can be used to reason about logic, where they represent proofs, and computation, where they represent programs. With the rise of interest in quantum cryptography and quantum computation, it became clear that there is extensive network of analogies between physics, topology, logic and computation. In this expository paper, we make some of these analogies precise using the concept of "closed symmetric monoidal category". We assume no prior knowledge of category theory, proof theory or computer science.

  • Piecewise-linear Ricci curvature flows on weighted graphs
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Community detection is an important problem in graph neural networks. Recently, algorithms based on Ricci curvature flows have gained significant attention. It was suggested by Ollivier (2009), and applied to community detection by Ni et al (2019) and Lai et al (2022). Its mathematical theory was due to Bai et al (2024) and Li-M\"unch (2025). In particular, solutions to some of these flows have existence, uniqueness and convergence. However, a unified theoretical framework has not yet been established in this field. In the current study, we propose several unified piecewise-linear Ricci curvature flows with respect to arbitrarily selected Ricci curvatures. First, we prove that the flows have global existence and uniqueness. Second, we show that if the Ricci curvature being used is homogeneous, then after undergoing multiple surgeries, the evolving graph has a constant Ricci curvature on each connected component. Note that five commonly used Ricci curvatures, which were respectively defined by Ollivier, Lin-Lu-Yau, Forman, Menger and Haantjes, are all homogeneous, and that the proof of all these results is independent of the choice of the specific Ricci curvature. Third, as an application, we apply the discrete piecewise-linear Ricci curvature flow with surgeries to the problem of community detection. On three real-world datasets, the flow consistently outperforms baseline models and existing methods. Complementary experiments on synthetic graphs further confirm its scalability and robustness. Compared with existing algorithms, our algorithm has two advantages: it does not require curvature calculations at each iteration, and the iterative process converges.

  • Pontrjagin dual in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Pontryagin duality establishes a contravariant equivalence between the category of abelian Hausdorff locally compact topological groups and its own dual category, where the dual of a group \(A\) is defined as the group of continuous homomorphisms from \(A\) to the circle group \(S^1\), equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. This duality implies that the dual of a discrete group is compact, the dual of a compact group is discrete, and the dual of a finite group is finite, with finite cyclic groups being self-dual. For abelian locally compact groups, the natural map from a group to the dual of its dual is an isomorphism, and the Fourier transform provides a Hilbert space isomorphism between function spaces on the group and its dual using Haar measures. The theory extends to higher structures such as 2-groups and group stacks, underpinning frameworks in equivariant K-theory and topological T-duality, while preserving key properties like second countability and separability under duality.

  • Pontryagin duality - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Pontryagin duality establishes a natural isomorphism between any locally compact abelian group and its dual, defined as the group of continuous homomorphisms to the circle group equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. This theorem generalizes Fourier analysis to include finite abelian groups, the integers, the real numbers, and p-adic fields, unifying observations about periodic, continuous, and discrete transforms. The duality relies on Haar measure for integration and extends the concept of dual spaces to topological groups, where the group and its dual are not naturally isomorphic but their endomorphism rings are opposite. A canonical isomorphism exists between a group and its double dual, making the duality functorial and exact. The theory depends on foundational work by Alfréd Haar, Raymond Paley, Norbert Wiener, and John von Neumann regarding measures and harmonic analysis. While classical duality applies to locally compact groups, generalizations exist for non-locally compact groups such as products and inverse limits, though a fundamental result by Martín-Peinador proves that any Hausdorff abelian group satisfying Pontryagin duality with a jointly continuous pairing must be locally compact.

  • Shifted Symplectic Structures
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    This is the first of a series of papers about \emph{quantization} in the context of \emph{derived algebraic geometry}. In this first part, we introduce the notion of \emph{$n$-shifted symplectic structures}, a generalization of the notion of symplectic structures on smooth varieties and schemes, meaningful in the setting of derived Artin n-stacks. We prove that classifying stacks of reductive groups, as well as the derived stack of perfect complexes, carry canonical 2-shifted symplectic structures. Our main existence theorem states that for any derived Artin stack $F$ equipped with an $n$-shifted symplectic structure, the derived mapping stack $\textbf{Map}(X,F)$ is equipped with a canonical $(n-d)$-shifted symplectic structure as soon a $X$ satisfies a Calabi-Yau condition in dimension $d$. These two results imply the existence of many examples of derived moduli stacks equipped with $n$-shifted symplectic structures, such as the derived moduli of perfect complexes on Calabi-Yau varieties, or the derived moduli stack of perfect complexes of local systems on a compact and oriented topological manifold. We also show that Lagrangian intersections carry canonical (-1)-shifted symplectic structures.

    Alexandre Grothendieck outlines a research programme initiated in 1972 to develop mathematical projects beyond university teaching, which he found increasingly illusory. For torus knots and many hyperbolic knots we show the subspace can be taken to be the orbit of a single maximally symmetric placement of the knot under the action of SO(4) by rotations of the ambient 3-sphere.   • spectrum in nLab

    This source defines a topological spectrum as an object in the universal stable (∞,1)-category \(Sp(Top)\) that stabilizes the category of topological spaces or ∞-groupoids under loop space and suspension operations, allowing homotopy groups to be non-trivial in negative degrees. Spectra with vanishing negative-degree homotopy groups are termed connective spectra, equivalent to infinite loop spaces and identifiable with non-negatively graded chain complexes via the Dold-Kan correspondence. The text distinguishes sequential pre-spectra, defined as sequences of pointed spaces with structure maps, from \(\Omega\)-spectra where these maps are isomorphisms, noting that \(\Omega\)-spectra serve as fibrant objects in a model structure. Various models for spectra exist and are Quillen equivalent, presenting the same stable homotopy theory, while the notion is attributed to G. W. Whitehead and Frank Adams, with modern developments surveyed in recent lecture notes and reviews.

It lists examples including derived algebraic, noncommutative, smooth, symplectic, Klein, and Cartan geometries. Regarding symplectic orbifolds, the text defines them as orbifolds with symplectic structures potentially featuring singularities modeled on fixed points of local finite group actions. It cites foundational work by Leonor Godinho on blowing up symplectic orbifolds and Weimin Chen on resolving them with applications to finite group actions. Additional references cover orbifold cohomology, including Hochschild cohomology of quantized symplectic orbifolds by Dolgushev and Etingof, equivariant cohomology for Hamiltonian torus actions by Holm and Matsumura, and holomorphic orbi-discs and Lagrangian Floer cohomology by Cho and Poddar.

  • Tensor network states and geometry
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Tensor network states are used to approximate ground states of local Hamiltonians on a lattice in D spatial dimensions. Different types of tensor network states can be seen to generate different geometries. Matrix product states (MPS) in D=1 dimensions, as well as projected entangled pair states (PEPS) in D>1 dimensions, reproduce the D-dimensional physical geometry of the lattice model; in contrast, the multi-scale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA) generates a (D+1)-dimensional holographic geometry. Here we focus on homogeneous tensor networks, where all the tensors in the network are copies of the same tensor, and argue that certain structural properties of the resulting many-body states are preconditioned by the geometry of the tensor network and are therefore largely independent of the choice of variational parameters. Indeed, the asymptotic decay of correlations in homogeneous MPS and MERA for D=1 systems is seen to be determined by the structure of geodesics in the physical and holographic geometries, respectively; whereas the asymptotic scaling of entanglement entropy is seen to always obey a simple boundary law -- that is, again in the relevant geometry. This geometrical interpretation offers a simple and unifying framework to understand the structural properties of, and helps clarify the relation between, different tensor network states. In addition, it has recently motivated the branching MERA, a generalization of the MERA capable of reproducing violations of the entropic boundary law in D>1 dimensions.

    Given a coherent sheaf on a smooth projective hypersurface X, we prove an explicit formula for its Chern character as a Cech cocycle in terms of the free resolution of the associated module and calculate its image in the Jacobian ring under the Griffiths residue map. The formula is a geometric analogue of the Kapustin-Li formula for Landau-Ginzburg models, but proven directly using Hodge-theoretic techniques. This yields an effective method to compute the primitive part of the Chern character of any coherent sheaf using commutative algebra. We finish by proving the Hodge conjecture for the degree 33 Fermat fourfold.

The work establishes a mathematical framework utilizing K-theory, Clifford algebras, and index theory to analyze physical systems described by quadratic Hamiltonians and specific symmetries. The thesis systematically classifies zero-dimensional, one-dimensional, and two-dimensional systems, including the Majorana chain, the integer quantum Hall effect, and the honeycomb lattice model. It assumes prior knowledge of algebraic topology and introductory quantum mechanics. The document serves as a partial fulfillment of the Bachelor of Arts with Honors requirements in the Mathematics Department.

  • The period-index conjecture is false for motivic reasons
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    For any integer $d \geq 3$ and any algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $0$ and transcendence degree at least $d-3$, or of characteristic $p>2$ and transcendence degree at least $d-2$, we construct a $d$-dimensional variety over $k$ with a Brauer class of period $2$ and index $2^d$, violating the period-index conjecture; in particular, the period-index conjecture fails in dimension $3$ over $\overline{\mathbf{Q}}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{F}_p(t)}$, and in all dimensions $d \geq 3$ over $\mathbf{C}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{F}_p((t))}$. To bound the index of Brauer classes from below, we employ an obstruction of motivic nature, which requires proving the nonexistence of integral Hodge or Tate classes satisfying a certain equation modulo $2$. Motivated by these counterexamples, we propose a period-index conjecture with corrections at small primes and, as evidence, prove its Hodge-theoretic counterpart.

  • The Sheaf Laplacian: A Topological Framework for Data Fusion and Consensus in Distributed Sensing Networks
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We argue here that traditional network models, which are overwhelmingly based on the mathematical construct of a simple graph, are fundamentally insufficient for capturing the complexity of modern distributed systems. Such systems are characterized by heterogeneous agents with diverse capabilities, high-dimensional and multi-modal data streams, and intricate, context-dependent relationships that cannot be adequately described by a simple connection or a scalar weight. The limitations of these classical models necessitate a new mathematical language, one with far greater expressive power. We have found that sheaf theory provides us with such a language. Moreover, we show that the sheaf Laplacian is a suitable mechanism for data fusion and establishing consensus within distributed sensing networks.

  • Universality in the 2D Ising model and conformal invariance of fermionic observables
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    It is widely believed that the celebrated 2D Ising model at criticality has a universal and conformally invariant scaling limit, which is used in deriving many of its properties. However, no mathematical proof of universality and conformal invariance has ever been given, and even physics arguments support (a priori weaker) M\"obius invariance. We introduce discrete holomorphic fermions for the 2D Ising model at criticality on a large family of planar graphs. We show that on bounded domains with appropriate boundary conditions, those have universal and conformally invariant scaling limits, thus proving the universality and conformal invariance conjectures.

  • A Formal Logic for Formal Category Theory
    maxsnew.comPDF documentsSource abstract
    Summary

    We present a domain-specific type theory for constructions and proofs in category theory. The type theory axiomatizes notions of category, functor, profunctor and a generalized form of natural trans- formations. The type theory imposes an ordered linear restriction on standard predicate logic, which guarantees that all functions between categories are functorial, all relations are profunctorial, and all trans- formations are natural by construction, with no separate proofs neces- sary. Important category theoretic proofs such as the Yoneda lemma and Co-yoneda lemma become simple type theoretic proofs about the rela- tionship between unit, tensor and (ordered) function types, and can be seen to be ordered refinements of theorems in predicate logic. The type theory is sound and complete for a categorical model in virtual equip- ments, which model both internal and enriched category theory. While the proofs in our type theory look like standard set-based arguments, the syntactic discipline ensure that all proofs and constructions carry over to enriched and internal settings as well.

  • A type theory for synthetic $\infty$-categories
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We propose foundations for a synthetic theory of $(\infty,1)$-categories within homotopy type theory. We axiomatize a directed interval type, then define higher simplices from it and use them to probe the internal categorical structures of arbitrary types. We define Segal types, in which binary composites exist uniquely up to homotopy; this automatically ensures composition is coherently associative and unital at all dimensions. We define Rezk types, in which the categorical isomorphisms are additionally equivalent to the type-theoretic identities - a "local univalence" condition. And we define covariant fibrations, which are type families varying functorially over a Segal type, and prove a "dependent Yoneda lemma" that can be viewed as a directed form of the usual elimination rule for identity types. We conclude by studying homotopically correct adjunctions between Segal types, and showing that for a functor between Rezk types to have an adjoint is a mere proposition. To make the bookkeeping in such proofs manageable, we use a three-layered type theory with shapes, whose contexts are extended by polytopes within directed cubes, which can be abstracted over using "extension types" that generalize the path-types of cubical type theory. In an appendix, we describe the motivating semantics in the Reedy model structure on bisimplicial sets, in which our Segal and Rezk types correspond to Segal spaces and complete Segal spaces.

  • A Universal Approach to Self-Referential Paradoxes, Incompleteness and Fixed Points
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Following F. William Lawvere, we show that many self-referential paradoxes, incompleteness theorems and fixed point theorems fall out of the same simple scheme. We demonstrate these similarities by showing how this simple scheme encompasses the semantic paradoxes, and how they arise as diagonal arguments and fixed point theorems in logic, computability theory, complexity theory and formal language theory.

  • Alternative to Grothendieck universes which is a conservative extension of ZFC?
    mathoverflow.netDiscussions and essays
    Summary

    The source argues that using Grothendieck universes in higher category theory is problematic because their existence relies on inaccessible cardinals, whose independence from ZFC cannot be proven. The author questions whether such large cardinals are fundamental or merely a convenient gadget, citing Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem as an example where this distinction matters. They seek an axiomatic class theory that is a conservative extension of ZFC, allowing seamless work with higher categories like stacks without assuming inaccessible cardinals. The author proposes a typed system where for every ordinal $\mu$, there are $\mu$-sets formed by unions of smaller sets, satisfying restricted ZFC axioms. They ask if such a theory exists, referencing NBG's conservativity, and request references to prior work on similar constructions, noting that the answer is likely negative but potentially unknown to mainstream algebraists.

  • anthropics/fermats-last-theorem
    github.comCode and software
    Summary

    This research artifact presents a complete, machine-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem for integers greater than or equal to 3, constructed entirely within the Lean 4 theorem prover using the Mathlib library. The proof synthesizes the work of Frey, Serre, Ribet, Wiles, and Taylor-Wiles, relying exclusively on Lean's three standard axioms without any unverified assumptions, placeholders, or native decision procedures. Its validity was rigorously confirmed through two independent verification methods: a replay of the entire proof against the Lean kernel by the 'comparator' tool, and a separate check by 'nanoda', an independent kernel written in Rust. The project also includes a comprehensive set of static web pages allowing offline browsing of all 29,511 theorems and 1,450 definition modules, with full attribution to the original mathematical sources and the AI agents used to generate the Lean code.

  • Axiom: The 1st Social Platform for Logically Valid Reasoning
    axiomreason.comOther websites
    Summary

    Axiom is an early-access platform designed to foster transparent and precise reasoning by requiring every argument to be grounded in explicitly stated premises and machine-checked proofs using the Lean 4 language. Unlike traditional online debates where definitions drift, Axiom's shared knowledge graph ensures that conclusions are independently verifiable and positions leading to contradictions are automatically invalidated, thereby dissolving unresolvable arguments. The system enforces that an argument stands only when a formal proof connects it to its stated axioms, regardless of the user's identity, effectively locking out inconsistent stances until revised. While the core logic requires technical proficiency with Lean 4, the platform integrates AI assistance to help beginners refine their thoughts without needing advanced mathematical knowledge. Users can operate locally with their own AI agents, though publishing work and participating in the public discourse requires a platform plan. By enforcing logical validity over subjective truth, Axiom aims to facilitate high-quality discourse across diverse topics, from philosophy to policy, ensuring that reasoning remains rigorous, auditable, and free from the manipulation common in unstructured online discussions.

  • Axiom: The 1st Social Platform for Logically Valid Reasoning

    This source defines a formal ontology for epistemic states, introducing rigid universal types such as Person, Belief, and BeliefSystem alongside processes like Observation and Inference. It establishes specific relations including CorrespondTo, HoldsBelief, and IsContradictory, where a belief is contradictory if it corresponds to both a proposition and its negation. The system further characterizes belief systems through predicates like ModelsPhysicalReality, IsContradictory, and Resolves, which determines if a system eliminates contradictions present in another.   • Chaitin's constant - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Chaitin's constant, also known as halting probability, is a real number representing the likelihood that a randomly constructed program halts, defined through a prefix-free universal computable function. This constant is characterized as normal, transcendental, and algorithmically random, yet it is fundamentally non-computable, meaning no algorithm can determine its digits. It holds a Turing equivalence to the halting problem, implying that knowing its first N bits resolves the halting problem for all programs of length up to N, effectively reducing undecidable problems to impossible ones. While the set of rationals less than the constant is computably enumerable, the set of rationals greater than it is not, classifying the constant as left-c.e. Its value varies depending on the specific encoding used, and it serves as a concrete example of an algorithmically random number within the arithmetical hierarchy, though it is not typical of all such numbers. The provided text is a bibliography listing academic references rather than a narrative source containing factual claims, methods, definitions, or limitations. It cites works by Barmpalias and Dowe on the universality probability of prefix-free machines, Calude's *Information and Randomness*, Downey and Hirschfeldt's *Algorithmic Randomness and Complexity*, and Li and Vitányi's *An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications*. Additional entries include survey articles on Chaitin's Omega, discussions on the limits of mathematical theories of everything, and Schmidhuber's work on limit-computable super-Omega. Since the excerpt consists solely of citation metadata such as authors, publication titles, years, publishers, and identifiers like ISBNs and DOIs, it does not present substantive research content to summarize in terms of findings or arguments.   • Chomsky hierarchy - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The Chomsky hierarchy classifies formal grammars into four nested types based on production rule constraints and computational power, originating from Noam Chomsky's 1956 work and later formalized with Marcel-Paul Schützenberger. Type-3 regular grammars, recognized by finite-state automata, generate languages definable by regular expressions, while Type-2 context-free grammars, accepted by pushdown automata, form the basis for most programming language syntax. Type-1 context-sensitive grammars, recognized by linear-bounded automata, require non-contracting rules, and Type-0 recursively enumerable grammars, equivalent to Turing machines, impose no restrictions on rules. This hierarchy demonstrates strict inclusions where each class properly contains the previous, yet natural language has been proven to exceed Type-2 context-free limits through phenomena like cross-serial dependencies in Swiss German, positioning it outside the standard formal classes despite its regularity violations.

  • Closed-world assumption - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The closed-world assumption (CWA) presumes that any statement not known to be true is false, contrasting with the open-world assumption where lack of knowledge does not imply falsity. In knowledge management, CWA applies when a database is complete or when a best definite answer is required from incomplete data, such as identifying editors who have not worked on a specific article. Raymond Reiter formalized this concept, often implemented via negation as failure, though adding negations of unproven atoms can introduce inconsistencies unless the knowledge base is in Horn form. Various formalizations exist, including generalized, extended, and careful CWA, with complexity ranging from polynomial to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. The partial-closed-world assumption offers an intermediate approach, allowing specific predicates to be treated under CWA while others remain open, balancing the credulousness of OWA with the rigidity of CWA in complex logical systems.

  • Computability logic - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Computability logic, introduced by Giorgi Japaridze in 2003, redefines logic as a formal theory of computability rather than static truth, treating formulas as computational problems modeled as games between a machine and an environment. This framework extends classical first-order logic with new operators such as parallel conjunction, choice disjunction, and branching recurrence to model diverse tasks including function computation and Turing reductions. Its main contribution lies in formulating validity as the guarantee of computability, providing constructive methods to derive algorithms directly from proofs without separate verification. The system operates as a conservative extension of classical logic and Peano arithmetic, preserving deductive power while characterizing specific interactive computational complexity classes through applied theories known as clarithmetics. Unlike traditional proof systems like natural deduction, alternative methods such as cirquent calculus are required to axiomatize nontrivial fragments and extract solutions. While this approach offers greater expressiveness and facilitates applications in constructive applied theories, it relies on alternative proof systems that differ significantly from standard natural deduction, and its complexity in modeling diverse computational tasks remains a challenge for broad adoption.

  • D. Organization
    www.danielgratzer.comPDF documents
    Summary

    This research extends Simplicial Type Theory to construct the category of Spaces, enabling synthetic arguments in $(\infty, 1)$-category theory without complex homotopy models. By integrating modalities such as `op` and `tw`, the authors define precategories, categories, and natural transformations, establishing that a precategory satisfies the Segal condition while a category requires canonical isomorphisms. Key contributions include constructing a fully faithful Yoneda embedding, proving that presheaf categories are the free cocompletion of a category, and demonstrating that the Yoneda embedding is dense. The work establishes the existence of pointwise Kan extensions, showing that pointwise left adjoints induce genuine adjunctions and that the free cocompletion is cocomplete. Furthermore, it proves that the inclusion of subcategories $S^{\le n}$ is a right adjoint, that every cocartesian fibration is proper, and that a functor is final if and only if the category of elements is final. These results provide empirical evidence that synthetic frameworks can derive difficult theorems with significantly greater conciseness than traditional approaches.

  • Di- is for Directed: First-Order Directed Type Theory via Dinaturality
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We show how dinaturality plays a central role in the interpretation of directed type theory where types are interpreted as (1-)categories and directed equality is represented by $\hom$-functors. We present a general elimination principle based on dinaturality for directed equality which very closely resembles the $J$-rule used in Martin-L\"of type theory, and we highlight which syntactical restrictions are needed to interpret this rule in the context of directed equality. We then use these rules to characterize directed equality as a left relative adjoint to a functor between (para)categories of dinatural transformations which contracts together two variables appearing naturally with a single dinatural one, with the relative functor imposing the syntactic restrictions needed. We then argue that the quantifiers of such a directed type theory should be interpreted as ends and coends, which dinaturality allows us to present in adjoint-like correspondences to a weakening functor. Using these rules we give a formal interpretation to Yoneda reductions and (co)end calculus, and we use logical derivations to prove the Fubini rule for quantifier exchange, the adjointness property of Kan extensions via (co)ends, exponential objects of presheaves, and the (co)Yoneda lemma. We show transitivity (composition), congruence (functoriality), and transport (coYoneda) for directed equality by closely following the same approach of Martin-L\"of type theory, with the notable exception of symmetry. We formalize our main theorems in Agda.

  • Displayed Type Theory and Semi-Simplicial Types
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We introduce Displayed Type Theory (dTT), a multi-modal homotopy type theory with discrete and simplicial modes. In the intended semantics, the discrete mode is interpreted by a model for an arbitrary $\infty$-topos, while the simplicial mode is interpreted by Reedy fibrant augmented semi-simplicial diagrams in that model. This simplicial structure is represented inside the theory by a primitive notion of display or dependency, guarded by modalities, yielding a partially-internal form of unary parametricity. Using the display primitive, we then give a coinductive definition, at the simplicial mode, of a type $\mathsf{SST}$ of semi-simplicial types. Roughly speaking, a semi-simplicial type $X$ consists of a type $X_0$ together with, for each $x:X_0$, a displayed semi-simplicial type over $X$. This mimics how simplices can be generated geometrically through repeated cones, and is made possible by the display primitive at the simplicial mode. The discrete part of $\mathsf{SST}$ then yields the usual infinite indexed definition of semi-simplicial types, both semantically and syntactically. Thus, dTT enables working with semi-simplicial types in full semantic generality.

  • Doctrinal Semantics of Directed First-Order Logic
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We present a first-order logic equipped with an "asymmetric" directed notion of equality, which can be thought of as rewrites between terms, allowing for types to be interpreted as preorders. The logic is equipped with a precise syntactic system of polarities, inspired by dinaturality, that keeps track of the occurrence of variables (positive/negative/both). We use this to give a characterization of directed equality as a relative left adjoint, generalizing the idea by Lawvere of equality as left adjoint; intuitively, the relativeness is used to capture the syntactic restriction that avoids symmetry of equality. The semantics of this logic and its system of variances is captured categorically using the notion of directed doctrine, which we prove sound and complete with respect to the syntax. Moreover, we prove that the classical fragment of our directed logic is complete with respect to a standard semantics in preorders.

    We answer the question whether all Heyting algebras can appear as the lattice of subterminal objects of an elementary topos in the negative. Concretely, we show that the free Heyting algebra on two generators, hence also on N generators for every N greater than 2, cannot be such a Heyting algebra. The mathematical results in this document were obtained with the help of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, although the document itself was written entirely by us, and we take full responsibility for its contents.

  • Formalizing Mathematics at Scale
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We present AutoformBot, a multi-agent system for building an Autoformalized Textbook Library At Scale (Atlas) in Lean 4. AutoformBot orchestrates thousands of LLM agents, equipped with formal verification tools, dependency-aware task scheduling, and collaborative version control, to translate informal textbook prose into machine-checked definitions and proofs. We apply our methods to a corpus of 26 open-access textbooks spanning analysis, algebra, topology, combinatorics, and probability, producing Atlas: a verified library of over 45,000 Lean 4 declarations and 500 thousand lines of code. We release two artifacts: (i) AutoformBot, the open-source multi-agent framework; and (ii) Atlas, the resulting formal library. Our results suggest that autoformalizing the core content of graduate-level mathematics at scale is now economically and technically feasible. This opens the door to the automated verification of both human- and machine-generated mathematics at a research level.

    Narya is a work-in-progress proof assistant currently implementing a normalization-by-evaluation algorithm and typechecker for a multi-modal type theory featuring observational-style Id/Bridge types that satisfy either parametricity or fibrancy/univalence. The system supports advanced features including user-definable mixfix notations, record types, inductive and coinductive datatypes, type families, and functions defined via matching and comatching case trees, alongside capabilities for separate compilation, hole solving, and a ProofGeneral interaction mode.   • Hazelnut: A Bidirectionally Typed Structure Editor Calculus
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Structure editors allow programmers to edit the tree structure of a program directly. This can have cognitive benefits, particularly for novice and end-user programmers. It also simplifies matters for tool designers, because they do not need to contend with malformed program text. This paper defines Hazelnut, a structure editor based on a small bidirectionally typed lambda calculus extended with holes and a cursor. Hazelnut goes one step beyond syntactic well-formedness: its edit actions operate over statically meaningful incomplete terms. Naively, this would force the programmer to construct terms in a rigid "outside-in" manner. To avoid this problem, the action semantics automatically places terms assigned a type that is inconsistent with the expected type inside a hole. This safely defers the type consistency check until the term inside the hole is finished. Hazelnut is a foundational type-theoretic account of typed structure editing, rather than an end-user tool itself. To that end, we describe how Hazelnut's rich metatheory, which we have mechanized in Agda, guides the definition of an extension to the calculus. We also discuss various plausible evaluation strategies for terms with holes, and in so doing reveal connections with gradual typing and contextual modal type theory, the Curry-Howard interpretation of contextual modal logic. Finally, we discuss how Hazelnut's semantics lends itself to implementation as a functional reactive program. Our reference implementation is written using js_of_ocaml.

  • Independence and Large Cardinals
    plato.stanford.eduReference material
    Summary

    This source explores the intricate relationship between independence results, interpretability hierarchies, and large cardinal axioms within mathematical logic, specifically addressing how standard systems like Peano Arithmetic and ZFC handle undecidable statements. The main contribution is the definition of interpretability as a relation where one system translates into another, forming a hierarchy of strength that allows mathematicians to climb from weaker to stronger theories to settle complex problems like the Continuum Hypothesis. The approach involves classifying theories based on their ability to prove Π01-statements and categorizing independence into three types: Single Jump, No Jump, and Double Jump, noting that while natural examples exist for the first two, no known natural examples exist for the Double Jump. Large cardinal axioms, characterized by elementary embeddings and properties like measurability or supercompactness, are presented as a canonical method to navigate this hierarchy and compare theories across distinct domains, though the text acknowledges that their status as true mathematical truths remains philosophically debated and that certain extreme axioms, such as Reinhardt's, have been proven inconsistent.

We then show that, when the quasicategory is locally cartesian closed, it is possible to further endow such a tribe with enough structure for it to provide a model of Martin-L\"of type theory with $\Pi$-types.   • jfpsep07.dvi
    cs.au.dkPDF documentsSource abstract
    Summary

    We consider the problem of reconciling a dependently typed functional language with im- perative features such as mutable higher-order state, pointer aliasing, and non-termination. We propose Hoare Type Theory (HTT), which incorporates Hoare-style speciﬁcations into types, making it possible to statically track and enforce correct use of side eﬀects. The main feature of HTT is the Hoare type {P}x:A{Q} specifying computations with precondition P and postcondition Q that return a result of type A. Hoare types can be nested, combined with other types, and abstracted, leading to a smooth integration with higher-order functions and type polymorphism. We further show that in the presence of type polymorphism, it becomes possible to interpret the Hoare types in the “small footprint” manner, as advocated by Separation Logic, whereby speciﬁcations tightly describe the state required by the computation. We establish that HTT is sound and compositional, in the sense that separate veriﬁca- tions of individual program components suﬃce to ensure the correctness of the composite program.

  • Leanabell-Prover-V2: Verifier-integrated Reasoning for Formal Theorem Proving via Reinforcement Learning
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We introduce our Leanabell-Prover-V2, a 7B large language models (LLMs) that can produce formal theorem proofs in Lean 4, with verifier-integrated Long Chain-of-Thoughts (CoT). Following our previous work Leanabell-Prover-V1, we continual to choose to posttrain existing strong prover models for further performance improvement. In our V2 version, we mainly upgrade the Reinforcement Learning (RL) with feedback provided by the Lean 4 verifier. Crucially, verifier feedback, such as indicating success or detailing specific errors, allows the LLM to become ``self-aware'' of the correctness of its own reasoning process and learn to reflexively correct errors. Leanabell-Prover-V2 directly optimizes LLM reasoning trajectories with multi-turn verifier interactions, together with feedback token masking for stable RL training and a simple reward strategy. Experiments show that Leanabell-Prover-V2 improves performance by 3.2% (pass@128) with Kimina-Prover-Preview-Distill-7B and 2.0% (pass@128) with DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B on the MiniF2F test set. The source codes, curated data and models are available at: https://github.com/Leanabell-LM/Leanabell-Prover-V2.

  • LeanAgent: Lifelong Learning for Formal Theorem Proving
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Large Language Models (LLMs) have been successful in mathematical reasoning tasks such as formal theorem proving when integrated with interactive proof assistants like Lean. Existing approaches involve training or fine-tuning an LLM on a specific dataset to perform well on particular domains, such as undergraduate-level mathematics. These methods struggle with generalizability to advanced mathematics. A fundamental limitation is that these approaches operate on static domains, failing to capture how mathematicians often work across multiple domains and projects simultaneously or cyclically. We present LeanAgent, a novel lifelong learning framework for formal theorem proving that continuously generalizes to and improves on ever-expanding mathematical knowledge without forgetting previously learned knowledge. LeanAgent introduces several key innovations, including a curriculum learning strategy that optimizes the learning trajectory in terms of mathematical difficulty, a dynamic database for efficient management of evolving mathematical knowledge, and progressive training to balance stability and plasticity. LeanAgent successfully generates formal proofs for 155 theorems across 23 diverse Lean repositories where formal proofs were previously missing, many from advanced mathematics. It performs significantly better than the static LLM baseline, proving challenging theorems in domains like abstract algebra and algebraic topology while showcasing a clear progression of learning from basic concepts to advanced topics. In addition, we analyze LeanAgent's superior performance on key lifelong learning metrics. LeanAgent achieves exceptional scores in stability and backward transfer, where learning new tasks improves performance on previously learned tasks. This emphasizes LeanAgent's continuous generalizability and improvement, explaining its superior theorem-proving performance.

Weak Vop\v{e}nka's Principle was already known to imply the existence of a proper class of measurable cardinals. We improve this lower bound to the optimal one by defining structures whose nontrivial homomorphisms can be used as extenders, thereby producing elementary embeddings witnessing C-strongness of some cardinal.

We use techniques of modal logic to formalize the logic of Reverse Mathematics into a system that we name s-logic. We argue that s-logic captures precisely the "logical" content of the implication and nonimplication relations between subsystems in Reverse Mathematics. By interpreting this theory internally within the classifying topos of 0-truncated strict intervals, he axiomatizes generic directed intervals to construct standard simplices and simplicial operators, enabling the inductive definition of Segal maps and the characterization of Rezk types as generalized univalence axioms. This hybrid approach reifies categories as directed spaces, mimicking the simplicial nature of Rezk categories externally while maintaining the algebraic structure of globular infinity-categories internally. Although the framework successfully defines codiscrete and discrete objects via higher inductive types and proposes specific classifiers for Cartesian opfibrations and fibrations, it faces significant challenges in incorporating cohesiveness into internal type theory and characterizing subtypes of the universe. Current formalization efforts in Coq have defined standard simplices and Segal types, yet proofs regarding the associativity and unitality of homotopy-coherent simplicial operators remain incomplete due to inherent technical complexities.

We capitalize on recent work by Gratzer et al. defining the $(\infty,1)$-category of $\infty$-groupoids in STT to define presheaf categories within STT and systematically develop their theory.   • Topological Quantum Gates in Homotopy Type Theory
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Despite the evident necessity of topological protection for realizing scalable quantum computers, the conceptual underpinnings of topological quantum logic gates had arguably remained shaky, both regarding their physical realization as well as their information-theoretic nature. Building on recent results on defect branes in string/M-theory and on their holographically dual anyonic defects in condensed matter theory, here we explain how the specification of realistic topological quantum gates, operating by anyon defect braiding in topologically ordered quantum materials, has a surprisingly slick formulation in parameterized point-set topology, which is so fundamental that it lends itself to certification in modern homotopically typed programming languages, such as cubical Agda. We propose that this remarkable confluence of concepts may jointly kickstart the development of topological quantum programming proper as well as of real-world application of homotopy type theory, both of which have arguably been falling behind their high expectations; in any case, it provides a powerful paradigm for simulating and verifying topological quantum computing architectures with high-level certification languages aware of the actual physical principles of realistic topological quantum hardware. In a companion article, we will explain how further passage to "dependent linear" homotopy data types naturally extends this scheme to a full-blown quantum programming/certification language in which our topological quantum gates may be compiled to verified quantum circuits, complete with quantum measurement gates and classical control.

The concept serves as a practical foundation for formalizing mathematical structures in proof assistants, often appearing as record types or type classes in literature by authors such as Coen & Tassi (2008) and Garillot et al.     Homotopy type theory presents an intensional framework where identity types function as path space objects, enabling the construction of homotopy fibers and equivalences between types. Central to this system is the univalence axiom, which equates the identity type of two types with the type of equivalences between them, thereby internalizing the principle that isomorphic types are identical. This principle implies function extensionality and allows deducing homotopy levels of universes, such as showing that a univalent Tarski universe of n-types is an (n+1)-type. The text details multiple equivalent formulations of univalence, including those requiring function extensionality or expressed via inference rules for definitional univalence, and discusses their consistency with resizing universes. Furthermore, it establishes the categorical semantics of dependent types within locally cartesian closed model categories, interpreting identity types as path objects and demonstrating how path induction arises from the universal property of pullbacks and fibrant replacements in these models. While the axiom holds in specific models like Tarski universes and elegant Reedy presheaves, it does not yet fully establish validity in the internal type theory of all (infinity,1)-toposes due to the lack of a sufficiently strict model for the object classifier.

  • Von Neumann universe - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The von Neumann universe, denoted by V, represents the class of hereditary well-founded sets formalized within Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (ZFC) as a cumulative hierarchy indexed by ordinal numbers. Defined through transfinite recursion, each stage Vα comprises all sets with a rank strictly less than α, relying fundamentally on the axiom of foundation and the integrity of ordinal numbers and transfinite induction. While finite stages exhibit tetrational growth that renders them physically unwritable beyond stage 5, V itself is a proper class rather than a set due to Russell's paradox, meaning its existence cannot be proven within ZFC. Although often attributed to von Neumann, the concept originated with Peano and was first published by Zermelo in 1930, with the notation V predating von Neumann. The provided text serves as a bibliography of eight academic sources, including foundational works by von Neumann, Whitehead and Russell, and Zermelo, which document historical developments in set theory but do not present original research findings or new theoretical claims. Consequently, the excerpt functions solely as a citation list without offering substantive content on the mathematical arguments or limitations found within the cited works.

  • When Bi-interpretability implies Synonymy
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Two salient notions of sameness of theories are synonymy, also known as definitional equivalence, and bi-interpretability. Of these two definitional equivalence is the strictest notion. In which cases can we infer synonymy from bi-interpretability? We study this question for the case of sequential theories. Our result is as follows. Suppose that two sequential theories are bi-interpretable and that the interpretations involved in the bi-interpretation are one-dimensional and identity preserving. Then, the theories are synonymous. The crucial ingredient of our proof is a version of the Schr\"oder-Bernstein theorem under very weak conditions. We think this last result has some independent interest. We provide an example to show that this result is optimal. There are two finitely axiomatized sequential theories that are bi-interpretable but not synonymous, where precisely one of the interpretations involved in the bi-interpretation is not identity preserving.

    Recent mathematical research has definitively disproved several major conjectures related to the Jacobian Conjecture (JC) in dimensions three and higher. Levent Alpöge provided a specific polynomial map in dimension 3 that serves as a counterexample to JC, demonstrating that a map can have a constant non-zero Jacobian determinant while failing to be injective. This result immediately invalidates the Mathieu Conjecture for the Lie group SU(3), as the latter implies JC in that dimension. Furthermore, the failure of JC in dimension 3 necessitates the falsity of the Gaussian Moments Conjecture (GMC) in some finite dimension, the Zhao's Vanishing Conjecture in some finite dimension, and the Image Conjecture in some finite dimension. While these results confirm that these conjectures do not hold universally, the provided sources only establish their existence of failure in specific dimensions without identifying the smallest dimension where each conjecture breaks down, leaving the precise minimal counterexamples for GMC, Zhao's conjecture, and the Image Conjecture as open problems.

    github.comCode and software
    Summary

    This research provides a definitive counterexample to Grothendieck's Power Question, which posits that a finite locally free group scheme of rank \(n\) should be annihilated by its \(n\)-th power word. The author constructs a specific rank-four group scheme \(G\) over a local Artin ring \(R = \mathbb{Z}[a,b]/(a^3,b^3,a^2b+2)\) by defining a Hopf algebra \(A\) as a corrected matched product of two order-two Oort–Tate group schemes. While the special fiber of \(G\) is the commutative group \(\alpha_2 \times \alpha_2\), the scheme itself is noncommutative due to nilpotent coefficients in the base, a condition necessary for the counterexample. The construction modifies the standard matched product ansatz by introducing a specific correction term \(q=b^2\) to resolve a failure in the cross condition, ensuring the resulting structure is a finite locally free group scheme. The primary contribution is the explicit demonstration that the fourth power map yields a nonzero result for the element \(U\), specifically \([4]^\#(U)=2bUV\), thereby proving that the \(n\)-th power word does not necessarily annihilate such schemes. The work highlights that while the conjecture holds for reduced bases and commutative schemes, it fails in the presence of nonreduced bases and noncommutativity, establishing the first known counterexample to the general conjecture.

  • Lawvere theory in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Lawvere theories, introduced by Bill Lawvere in 1963, provide a categorical framework for universal algebra that generalizes structures such as groups, rings, and associative algebras. Defined as categories with finite products where objects are powers of a generic object, these theories model finitary operations via hom-sets, establishing an equivalence between the category of algebras and product-preserving functors to a base category like Set. The approach characterizes algebraic structures through monadic functors that preserve filtered colimits, linking definable operations to universally quantified equations and demonstrating that categories of algebras always possess small limits and filtered colimits. However, the framework has notable limitations; while it successfully characterizes classes closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras, and products, it cannot fully describe certain structures like fields or integral domains which lack products or require infinitary axioms. Furthermore, although the theory handles congruences and free algebras via filtered colimits of representables, the generalization of Higman's embedding theorem to all single-sorted algebraic theories remains an unresolved open problem known as the Boone conjecture.

    This source defines the group homology of a k-linear G-representation A as the homology of a complex formed by direct sums of A indexed by tuples of group elements, with a specific differential involving the group action and permutation of group elements. It establishes a k-linear isomorphism between the inhomogeneous chain complex and the coinvariants of the tensor product of A with the bar resolution of k, proving that the resulting differential squares to zero. Consequently, the nth group homology H_n(G, A) is isomorphic to the nth left-derived functor Tor_n(A, k), where Tor is derived from the functor mapping pairs of representations to their coinvariants under the tensor product over k. The implementation avoids standard module instances over the group ring to prevent scalar action conflicts and specializes to low degrees in a separate file, while noting future work on upgrading these isomorphisms to derived functor level.

    In mathematics, a quiver is a multidigraph used in representation theory to define structures like vector spaces and linear maps on vertices and arrows, forming the basis for path algebras and quiver varieties. While quivers lack composition and identity morphisms, they relate to categories via free functors and can be generalized within any category C as functors from a specific free quiver. Key concepts include representations, which form a category, and the classification of finite-type quivers through Gabriel's theorem linking them to ADE Dynkin diagrams. Extensions include quivers with relations, reflexive quivers, and their applications in cluster algebras and derived noncommutative geometry, with foundational work by Gabriel, Dlab, Ringel, and Kac establishing connections to Lie algebras and root systems.

  • 528-5.dvi
    www.stat.purdue.eduPDF documents
    Summary

    Research on point estimation focuses on selecting estimators with low bias and variability to construct shorter confidence intervals, utilizing foundational concepts developed by R.A. Fisher such as the likelihood function, maximum likelihood estimates (MLE), sufficient statistics, and Fisher information. The likelihood function serves as the basis for MLE, though its properties vary significantly; while often unimodal, it can be bimodal or non-differentiable, and MLEs may not always exist or be unique outside regular exponential families. Fisher information measures estimator precision but is not invariant under reparameterization, while sufficient statistics capture all parameter information in the data, with minimal sufficient statistics being most parsimonious and uniquely characterized in regular exponential families. Basu's Theorem establishes the independence between minimal sufficient statistics and ancillary statistics, enabling Rao-Blackwellization to improve estimators by conditioning on sufficient statistics, while the Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem provides a method for constructing Uniformly Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimators (UMVUE) within exponential families. Additionally, the Cramér-Rao inequality establishes a lower bound on estimator variance based on Fisher information, which quantifies precision and generalizes to multiparameter settings via a matrix form, though equality in this bound often fails for parameters other than linear functions of sufficient statistics in exponential families.

  • Bayesian Networks, Markov Networks, Moralisation, Triangulation: a Categorical Perspective
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Moralisation and Triangulation are transformations allowing to switch between different ways of factoring a probability distribution into a graphical model. Moralisation allows to view a Bayesian network (a directed model) as a Markov network (an undirected model), whereas triangulation addresses the opposite direction. We present a categorical framework where these transformations are modelled as functors between a category of Bayesian networks and one of Markov networks. The two kinds of network (the objects of these categories) are themselves represented as functors from a `syntax' domain to a `semantics' codomain. Notably, moralisation and triangulation can be defined inductively on such syntax via functor pre-composition. Moreover, while moralisation is fully syntactic, triangulation relies on semantics. This leads to a discussion of the variable elimination algorithm, reinterpreted here as a functor in its own right, that splits the triangulation procedure in two: one purely syntactic, the other purely semantic. This approach introduces a functorial perspective into the theory of probabilistic graphical models, which highlights the distinctions between syntactic and semantic modifications.

  • Bayesian reasoning in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Bayesian reasoning applies probability theory to inductive and abductive reasoning by interpreting probabilities as expressions of an agent's uncertainty rather than objective chance, effectively generalizing deductive logic where truth corresponds to probabilities of 1 and 0. This perspective allows rational degrees of belief for settled but unknown propositions, such as the value of natural constants or past coin tosses, and is justified by Dutch Book arguments which show that violating probability axioms leads to guaranteed financial loss. While some critics find the reliance on financial loss unbefitting for logic, axiomatic approaches like Cox's theorem and principles such as maximum entropy or the principle of indifference offer alternative justifications. Degrees of belief are updated via Bayes' Rule upon receiving evidence, a process known as conditionalizing, though assigning priors remains challenging when hypotheses are not exhaustive. De Finetti's Representation Theorem further formalizes repeated sampling by linking exchangeable sequences to mixtures of Bernoulli distributions, though generalizations exist for Markov chains where outcomes may depend on predecessors.

  • Black box - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The Black Box theory, formalized by W. Ross Ashby and Norbert Wiener in mid-20th-century cybernetics, posits that systems with inaccessible internal mechanisms can be effectively analyzed and controlled by focusing solely on observable input-output relationships. This approach treats complex entities as opaque, allowing for prediction and pattern recognition without requiring knowledge of underlying causal structures, a method applicable across engineering, biology, psychology, medicine, and computing. While the theory simplifies the study of proprietary or intricate systems by assuming only temporal precedence between inputs and outputs, it faces a fundamental limitation: multiple distinct internal structures can produce identical external behaviors, rendering the unique determination of internal causes impossible. Despite ongoing research into internal mechanisms, the theory remains a practical tool for managing complexity by prioritizing stimulus-response patterns over structural inspection, effectively contrasting with white box methods that demand full internal knowledge.

  • Closing the Oracle-Complexity Gap in Derivative-Free Convex Optimization: A Near-Quadratic Lower Bound from Exact Function Values
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We study the deterministic query complexity of minimizing a convex Lipschitz function over a $d$-dimensional Euclidean ball using only exact function values. At accuracy $\Theta(d^{-1/2})$, the previously applicable lower bound was $\Omega(d)$, inherited from the stronger full first-order oracle, while an upper bound from Protasov's value-only method requires $O(d^2\log^2 d)$ evaluations. By providing a lower bound of $\Omega(\,\frac{d^2}{\log(d+1)})$ on the oracle complexity in this setting, we thereby close this gap dating back to 1996, up to polylogarithmic factors. Furthermore, we are able to lift this result to the mixed-integer setting: Mixed-integer convex optimization with $d$ continuous and $n$ discrete variables using function values requires $\tilde{\Omega}(d^2\cdot 2^n)$ queries.

  • Delocalization of One-Dimensional Random Band Matrices
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Consider an $ N \times N$ Hermitian one-dimensional random band matrix with band width $W > N^{1 / 2 + \frak c} $ for any $ {\frak c} > 0$. In the bulk of the spectrum and in the large $ N $ limit, we obtain the following results: (i) The semicircle law holds up to the scale $ N^{-1 + \varepsilon} $ for any $ \varepsilon > 0 $. (ii) All $ L^2 $- normalized eigenvectors are delocalized, meaning their $ L^\infty$ norms are simultaneously bounded by $ N^{-\frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon} $ with overwhelming probability, for any $ \varepsilon > 0 $. (iii) Quantum unique ergodicity holds in the sense that the local $ L^2 $ mass of eigenvectors becomes equidistributed with high probability. (iv) Universality of eigenvalue statistics holds, i.e., the local eigenvalue statistics of these band matrices are given by those of Gaussian unitary ensembles.

  • Engineering Emergence
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    A defining property of complex systems is that they have multiscale structure. How does this multiscale structure come about? We argue that within systems there emerges a hierarchy of scales that contribute to a system's causal workings. An intuitive example is how a computer can be described at the level of its hardware circuitry (its microscale) but also its machine code (a mesoscale) and all the way up at its operating system (its macroscale). Here we show that even simple systems possess this kind of emergent hierarchy, which usually forms over only a small subset of the super-exponentially many possible scales of description. To capture this formally, we extend the theory of causal emergence (version 2.0) so as to analyze how causal contributions span the full multiscale structure of a system. Our analysis reveals that systems can be classified along a taxonomy of emergence, such as being either top-heavy or bottom-heavy in their causal workings. From this new taxonomy of emergence, we derive a measure of complexity based on a literal notion of scale-freeness (here, when causation is spread equally across the scales of a system) and compare this to the standard network science definition of scale-freeness based on degree distribution, showing the two are closely related. Finally, we demonstrate the ability to engineer not just the degree of emergence in a system, but to control it with pinpoint precision.

  • From Scattered Phase-Space Observations to an Empirical Fokker-Planck Equation: A Delaunay-Voronoi finite-volume construction
    zenodo.orgOther websites
    Summary

    A dynamical phase plane trajectory contains more than a sequence of state data. It records where the system has been, which way it moved, and how much each step has varied. We use these three observations to build a Delaunay-Voronoi Fokker-Planck (DVFP) description of a dynamical system from sparse or irregular phase-space data. The observed states define Voronoi control volumes, successive observations give the local mean motion, or drift, and the scatter around that motion gives diffusion. Because probability changes inside a cell only by crossing one of its faces, these ingredients lead directly to a finite-volume Fokker-Planck balance. We can then properly apply the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) framework afterward, to derive the equations of motion. Because the reconstruction supplies density, drift, diffusion, and the ingredients needed to estimate probability current from the observations, it also provides the ingredients needed for stochastic-thermodynamic analysis when such an interpretation is appropriate. The time-ordered Delaunay-Voronoi construction was introduced in our earlier market application. Here we separate it from that setting, state the probability balance in general form, and test the reconstruction on a stochastic damped oscillator whose dynamics are known in advance.

    Gregory John Chaitin, born in 1947, is an Argentine-American mathematician and computer scientist known for independently discovering algorithmic complexity alongside Kolmogorov and Solomonoff. He defined Chaitin's constant Ω in 1975, a real number representing the probability that a random program halts, which is definable but not computable. Chaitin also originated using graph coloring for register allocation in compiling. His work extends to metabiology and information-theoretic formalizations of evolution, where he claims algorithmic information theory can define life and consciousness. In epistemology, he argues that some mathematical facts are true by accident and should be accepted via a quasi-empirical methodology rather than proof. He has received numerous honors, including a Leibniz Medal in 2007 and honorary doctorates from the University of Maine and the National University of Córdoba.

  • Inference for Probabilistic Dependency Graphs
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Probabilistic dependency graphs (PDGs) are a flexible class of probabilistic graphical models, subsuming Bayesian Networks and Factor Graphs. They can also capture inconsistent beliefs, and provide a way of measuring the degree of this inconsistency. We present the first tractable inference algorithm for PDGs with discrete variables, making the asymptotic complexity of PDG inference similar that of the graphical models they generalize. The key components are: (1) the observation that, in many cases, the distribution a PDG specifies can be formulated as a convex optimization problem (with exponential cone constraints), (2) a construction that allows us to express these problems compactly for PDGs of boundeed treewidth, (3) contributions to the theory of PDGs that justify the construction, and (4) an appeal to interior point methods that can solve such problems in polynomial time. We verify the correctness and complexity of our approach, and provide an implementation of it. We then evaluate our implementation, and demonstrate that it outperforms baseline approaches. Our code is available at http://github.com/orichardson/pdg-infer-uai.

  • Information Geometry Connecting Wasserstein Distance and Kullback-Leibler Divergence via the Entropy-Relaxed Transportation Problem
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Two geometrical structures have been extensively studied for a manifold of probability distributions. One is based on the Fisher information metric, which is invariant under reversible transformations of random variables, while the other is based on the Wasserstein distance of optimal transportation, which reflects the structure of the distance between random variables. Here, we propose a new information-geometrical theory that is a unified framework connecting the Wasserstein distance and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. We primarily considered a discrete case consisting of $n$ elements and studied the geometry of the probability simplex $S_{n-1}$, which is the set of all probability distributions over $n$ elements. The Wasserstein distance was introduced in $S_{n-1}$ by the optimal transportation of commodities from distribution ${\mathbf{p}}$ to distribution ${\mathbf{q}}$, where ${\mathbf{p}}$, ${\mathbf{q}} \in S_{n-1}$. We relaxed the optimal transportation by using entropy, which was introduced by Cuturi. The optimal solution was called the entropy-relaxed stochastic transportation plan. The entropy-relaxed optimal cost $C({\mathbf{p}}, {\mathbf{q}})$ was computationally much less demanding than the original Wasserstein distance but does not define a distance because it is not minimized at ${\mathbf{p}}={\mathbf{q}}$. To define a proper divergence while retaining the computational advantage, we first introduced a divergence function in the manifold $S_{n-1} \times S_{n-1}$ of optimal transportation plans. We fully explored the information geometry of the manifold of the optimal transportation plans and subsequently constructed a new one-parameter family of divergences in $S_{n-1}$ that are related to both the Wasserstein distance and the KL-divergence.

    This source synthesizes diverse interpretations of probability, primarily critiquing the classical approach and Kolmogorov's axioms for their limitations in handling infinite spaces and circular reasoning regarding the principle of indifference.   • Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem establishes that every multivariate continuous real-valued function can be expressed as a finite superposition of continuous single-variable functions and addition, resolving Hilbert's thirteenth problem. While the theorem holds for continuous functions, it fails if all component functions are required to be continuously differentiable, though it remains valid if they are merely 1-Lipschitz continuous. Variants by Lorentz, Sprecher, and Ostrand reduce the number of outer or inner functions, and the theorem extends to compact metric spaces and discontinuous functions where inner functions remain universal. Practical applications in machine learning utilize Kolmogorov–Arnold networks, analogous to universal approximation theorems, despite limitations regarding the non-smoothness and wild behavior of the inner functions. A specific proof demonstrates that Kolmogorov–Arnold tuples form an open and dense subset of the function space, utilizing grid systems and the Baire category theorem to establish existence. The provided text is a bibliography listing academic references concerning Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and related mathematical theories, rather than a single coherent research article with specific experimental results or methodological details. It cites foundational work by Andrey Kolmogorov and Vladimir Arnold on representing continuous multivariate functions as superpositions of functions of fewer variables, alongside subsequent studies on neural network realizations and training by authors such as Lin, Unbehauen, Köppen, and Ismayilova. The list includes papers from journals like *Neural Computation* and *Neural Networks*, as well as lecture notes and arXiv preprints, covering topics from the original Hilbert's Thirteenth Problem to modern interpretations of these architectures for interpretability. No specific empirical findings, data sets, or proposed algorithms are described within this excerpt, as it serves solely as a citation list for the theoretical underpinnings and applications of Kolmogorov superposition theorems in artificial intelligence.

  • Mobility Edge for L\'evy Matrices
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    L\'evy matrices are symmetric random matrices whose entry distributions lie in the domain of attraction of an $\alpha$-stable law. For $\alpha < 1$, predictions from the physics literature suggest that high-dimensional L\'{e}vy matrices should display the following phase transition at a point $E_{\mathrm{mob}}$. Eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues in $(-E_{\mathrm{mob}},E_{\mathrm{mob}})$ should be delocalized, while eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues outside of this interval should be localized. Further, $E_{\mathrm{mob}}$ is given by the (presumably unique) positive solution to $\lambda(E,\alpha) =1$, where $\lambda$ is an explicit function of $E$ and $\alpha$. We prove the following results about high-dimensional L\'{e}vy matrices. (1) If $\lambda(E,\alpha) > 1$ then eigenvectors with eigenvalues near $E$ are delocalized. (2) If $E$ is in the connected components of the set $\big\{ x : \lambda(x,\alpha) < 1 \big\}$ containing $\pm \infty$, then eigenvectors with eigenvalues near $E$ are localized. (3) For $\alpha$ sufficiently near $0$ or $1$, there is a unique positive solution $E = E_{\mathrm{mob}}$ to $\lambda(E,\alpha) = 1$, demonstrating the existence of a (unique) phase transition. (a) If $\alpha$ is close to $0$, then $E_{\mathrm{mob}}$ scales approximately as $|\log \alpha|^{-2/\alpha}$. (b) If $\alpha$ is close to $1$, then $E_{\mathrm{mob}}$ scales as $(1-\alpha)^{-1}$. Our proofs proceed through an analysis of the local weak limit of a L\'{e}vy matrix, given by a certain infinite-dimensional, heavy-tailed operator on the Poisson weighted infinite tree.

    spacechimplives.substack.comEssays and blog posts
    Summary

    The source proposes a theoretical framework where constraints on a system's probability distribution are equated with increased energy and reduced entropy, suggesting that relaxing these constraints allows work to be performed as the system returns toward equilibrium.
