  • Natural Intelligence: the information processing power of life
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Merely by existing, all physical systems contain information, and physical dynamics transforms and processes that information. This note investigates the information processing power of living systems. Living systems harvest free energy from the sun, from geothermal sources, and from each other. They then use that free energy to drive the complex set of chemical interactions that underlie life. All molecules -- be they simple molecules such as water, or complex molecules such as DNA -- register information via their chemical composition. When these molecules undergo chemical reactions, that information is transformed and processed. These chemical transformations can be thought of as elementary logical operations: such bio-ops include the absorption of a photon in a chromophore during photosynthesis, the formation or breaking of covalent, hydrogen, and van der Waals bonds in the process of metabolism and reproduction, or the release of a neurotransmitter molecule when a synapse fires in the brain. This paper estimates the total number of bio-ops that have been, and are being performed, by life on earth. We find that the current number of bio-ops performed by all life on earth is around $10^{33}-10^{35}$ bio-ops per second. The cells in an individual human being perform around $10^{20}-10^{22}$ bio-ops per second, comparable to the information processing power of all the computers, cell phones, and server farms on earth. Depending on how one defines a neural operation, at most a few percent of human bio-ops take place in the firing of neurons and synapses in the brain. Over the course of life on earth, about $10^{50}-10^{52}$ bio-ops have taken place.

  • Plasticity as the Mirror of Empowerment
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Agents are minimally entities that are influenced by their past observations and act to influence future observations. This latter capacity is captured by empowerment, which has served as a vital framing concept across artificial intelligence and cognitive science. This former capacity, however, is equally foundational: In what ways, and to what extent, can an agent be influenced by what it observes? In this paper, we ground this concept in a universal agent-centric measure that we refer to as plasticity, and reveal a fundamental connection to empowerment. Following a set of desiderata on a suitable definition, we define plasticity using a new information-theoretic quantity we call the generalized directed information. We show that this new quantity strictly generalizes the directed information introduced by Massey (1990) while preserving all of its desirable properties. Under this definition, we find that plasticity is well thought of as the mirror of empowerment: The two concepts are defined using the same measure, with only the direction of influence reversed. Our main result establishes a tension between the plasticity and empowerment of an agent, suggesting that agent design needs to be mindful of both characteristics. We explore the implications of these findings, and suggest that plasticity, empowerment, and their relationship are essential to understanding agency

  • Possibilistic inferential models: a review
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    An inferential model (IM) is a model describing the construction of provably reliable, data-driven uncertainty quantification and inference about relevant unknowns. IMs and Fisher's fiducial argument have similar objectives, but a fundamental distinction between the two is that the former doesn't require that uncertainty quantification be probabilistic, offering greater flexibility and allowing for a proof of its reliability. Important recent developments have been made thanks in part to newfound connections with the imprecise probability literature, in particular, possibility theory. The brand of possibilistic IMs studied here are straightforward to construct, have very strong frequentist-like reliability properties, and offer fully conditional, Bayesian-like (imprecise) probabilistic reasoning. This paper reviews these key recent developments, describing the new theory, methods, and computational tools. A generalization of the basic possibilistic IM is also presented, making new and unexpected connections with ideas in modern statistics and machine learning, e.g., bootstrap and conformal prediction.

  • Principal component analysis - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference materialAccessible page excerpt
    Summary

    Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that transforms data into a new coordinate system where principal components, defined as unit vectors, capture the largest variance while remaining orthogonal. Mathematically, PCA is equivalent to the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the data matrix, where the right singular vectors correspond to the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and singular values represent the square roots of the eigenvalues. The method optimally retains the subspace with the largest variance through an orthogonal transformation, a property formalized by the Eckart–Young theorem which states that the truncated SVD provides the nearest rank-L approximation in the Frobenius norm. However, PCA is sensitive to variable scaling and assumes linear correlations, requiring mean-centering and standardization to ensure results are independent of units. While effective for pattern recognition and detecting near-constant linear relationships, it is not optimized for class separability and fails when non-linear structures are present, necessitating alternative methods like kernel PCA or linear discriminant analysis.

  • Singular Basins in Multiscale Systems: Tunneling between Stable States | Phys. Rev. Lett.
    journals.aps.orgOther websites
    Summary

    This research investigates 'singular basins' and 'singular funnels' in multiscale dynamical systems, identifying narrow geometric structures that enable transitions between stable states impossible to predict in reduced models. By analyzing adaptive phase rotator systems and mean-field coupled active rotators, the authors demonstrate that standard approximation techniques like adiabatic elimination and time averaging fail to capture these phenomena, often leading to incorrect conclusions regarding system resilience. The study utilizes low-dimensional canonical forms, Monte Carlo simulations, and geometric singular perturbation theory to show that while singular funnel volumes generally shrink with increasing timescale separation, they exhibit robust scaling and intricate patterns even in high-dimensional phase spaces. Ultimately, the findings emphasize the critical necessity of considering full-system dynamics rather than relying on dimensionality reduction to accurately predict rare but significant state changes and avoid missing critical transitions in complex adaptive networks.

  • teorth/analysis
    github.comCode and software
    Summary

    This repository presents a Lean formalization of the textbook Analysis I, structured as a faithful but unoptimized paraphrase rather than a direct replacement for the original text. Its primary contribution is to serve as an annotated companion that develops natural numbers independently in Chapter 2 before transitioning to Mathlib definitions for subsequent chapters, incorporating technical adjustments like zero-based indexing and total functions to handle undefined operations. The project includes comprehensive documentation for all chapters and appendices, though it explicitly excludes solutions to reader exercises. While the formalization also hosts unrelated formalizations such as Measure Theory and physical units, its maintenance requires careful management of the lakefile to conditionally pin Mathlib and doc-gen4 versions, necessitating incremental updates and manual reversion of the lean-toolchain to prevent unintended version shifts.

  • The New Math of How Large-Scale Order Emerges | Quanta Magazine
    www.quantamagazine.orgNews and articles
    Summary

    Researchers Fernando Rosas and colleagues propose a framework defining emergence as a hierarchical structure governed by 'computational closure,' where macroscopic behaviors are determined by rules independent of microscopic details. Using computational mechanics, they identify three types of closure—informational, causal, and computational—demonstrating that emergent systems possess nested, 'strongly lumpable' causal states where lower-level details do not aid macro-level prediction. The team validated this theory by testing it on model systems like random walks in city networks and artificial neural networks, finding that these systems exhibit the predicted hierarchical organization. While the framework successfully formalizes how large-scale patterns arise from complex interactions, the authors acknowledge limitations, noting that some living organisms, such as the human heart, may display 'leaky emergence' where microscopic variations still influence macroscopic outcomes. Additionally, related work by Hoel, Tononi, and others investigates causal emergence, arguing that higher-level patterns can possess greater causal power than micro-level details, challenging traditional reductionist views on causation and free will, though significant disagreement remains regarding whether macroscopic causation can genuinely drive microscopic processes.

  • The Opdam-Cherednik kernel is the Laplace transform of a positive measure
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We prove that the Opdam-Cherednik kernel, also known as the nonsymmetric Opdam hypergeometric function, can be written as the Laplace transform of a positive measure supported on the convex hull of the Weyl group orbit of its argument. As a consequence, the trigonometric Dunkl intertwining operator is positivity preserving. The main ingredient in the proof is a new formula for the Opdam-Cherednik kernel as a degeneration of nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials. As a further application, we prove majorization inequalities for Macdonald polynomials and Heckman-Opdam hypergeometric functions associated with arbitrary root systems.

  • The Rectangular Finite Free Heat Flow
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We define and study the rectangular finite free heat flow, a dynamical system on polynomials that plays the role of the heat equation in the setting of rectangular finite free probability. We show several equivalent characterizations of the evolution (including PDE and gradient flow formulations), establish basic properties of the dynamics, and determine the asymptotic distributions of the polynomial roots in the long-time and high-degree limits. We also discuss connections with Calogero-Moser systems and Dunkl processes, and we show that the rectangular finite free heat flow describes the mean curvature expansion of a family of compact Lie group orbits.

  • Theory of capacities
    aif.centre-mersenne.orgOther websitesSource abstract
    Summary

    Résumé C’est un essai de théorie générale des fonctions croissantes d’ensemble. On est amené à mettre en évidence diverses classes importantes de telles fonctions, en particulier la classe des fonctions fortement sous-additives, pour lesquelles existe une théorie analogue à celle de la mesure, et une sous-classe de celle-ci, à savoir la classe des fonctions alternées d’ordre infini, analogues aux fonctions numériques complètement monotones. La capacité classique est une telle fonction d’ensemble ; il en résulte l’identité des capacités intérieure et extérieure de tout ensemble borélien ou analytique. Un outil de recherche puissant est la représentation intégrale des fonctions d’une classe additive et convexe au moyen des éléments extrémaux d’une telle classe. Cette représentation permet d’identifier les fonctions alternées d’ordre infini avec certaines probabilités associées à l’ensemble variable.

  • Using Dynamical Systems Theory to Quantify Complexity in Asymptotic Lenia
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Continuous cellular automata (CCAs) have evolved from discrete lookup tables to continuous partial differential equation (PDE) formulations in the search for novel forms of complexity. Despite innovations in qualitative behavior, analytical methods have lagged behind, reinforcing the notion that emergent complexity defies simple explanation. In this paper, we demonstrate that the PDE formulation of Asymptotic Lenia enables rigorous analysis using dynamical systems theory. We apply the concepts of symmetries, attractors, Lyapunov exponents, and fractal dimensions to characterize complex behaviors mathematically. Our contributions include: (1) a mathematical explanation for the four distinct solution classes (solitons, rotators, periodic and chaotic patterns), (2) conditions for the existence of a global attractor with fractal dimension $>4$, (3) identification of Kaplan-Yorke dimension as an effective complexity measure for CCAs, and (4) an efficient open-source implementation for calculating Lyapunov exponents and the covariant Lyapunov vectors for CCAs. We conclude by identifying the minimal set of properties that enable complex behavior in a broader class of CCAs. This framework provides a foundation for understanding and measuring complexity in artificial life systems.

  • What is Entropy?
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    This short book is an elementary course on entropy, leading up to a calculation of the entropy of hydrogen gas at standard temperature and pressure. Topics covered include information, Shannon entropy and Gibbs entropy, the principle of maximum entropy, the Boltzmann distribution, temperature and coolness, the relation between entropy, expected energy and temperature, the equipartition theorem, the partition function, the relation between expected energy, free energy and entropy, the entropy of a classical harmonic oscillator, the entropy of a classical particle in a box, and the entropy of a classical ideal gas.

  • Why and How do Complex Systems Self-Organize at All? Average Action Efficiency as a Predictor, Measure, Driver, and Mechanism of Self-Organization
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Self-organization in complex systems is a process in which randomness is reduced and emergent structures appear that allow the system to function in a more competitive way with other states of the system or with other systems. It occurs only in the presence of energy gradients, facilitating energy transmission through the system and entropy production. Being a dynamic process, self-organization requires a dynamic measure and dynamic principles. The principles of decreasing unit action and increasing total action are two dynamic variational principles that are viable to utilize in a self-organizing system. Based on this, average action efficiency can serve as a quantitative measure of the degree of self-organization. Positive feedback loops connect this measure with all other characteristics of a complex system, providing all of them with a mechanism for exponential growth, and indicating power law relationships between each of them as confirmed by data and simulations. In this study, we apply those principles and the model to agent-based simulations. We find that those principles explain self-organization well and that the results confirm the model. By measuring action efficiency we can have a new answer to the question: "What is complexity and how complex is a system?". This work shows the explanatory and predictive power of those models, which can help understand and design better complex systems.

  • A proof of an identity for the critical exponents of jamming
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Within the full replica-symmetry-breaking (fullRSB) solution of dense hard spheres in infinite dimension, Charbonneau, Kurchan, Parisi, Urbani, and Zamponi (CKPUZ; J.Stat.Mech.P10009, 2014) introduced three critical exponents $a$, $b$, $c$ governing the matching region of the fullRSB profile near the jamming transition. These exponents satisfy two scaling relations. The first, $b=(1+c)/2$, was established analytically by the diffusion-drift balance in the scaling ansatz. The second, $a+b=1$, was observed numerically to arbitrary precision but could not be proven. The exponents $a,b,c$ of the scaling fullRSB ansatz are related to the physical exponents $\alpha, \theta, \kappa$ that control the gap, force, and overlap distributions by the relations $\alpha=a/b$, $\theta=(c-a)/(b-c)$, $\kappa=c+1$. Crucially, the relation $a+b=1$ yields the scaling relations $\alpha=1/(2+\theta)$ and $\kappa=2-2/(3+\theta)$ predicted on independent grounds by the mechanical-marginal-stability arguments of Wyart and collaborators. Here, we give an analytic proof of the identity $a+b=1$ from the scaling fullRSB equations. The proof was obtained through interaction with Claude (Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7) and verified by us.

  • Algebraic ER=EPR and Complexity Transfer
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We propose an algebraic definition of ER=EPR in the $G_N \to 0$ limit, which associates bulk spacetime connectivity/disconnectivity to the operator algebraic structure of a quantum gravity system. The new formulation not only includes information on the amount of entanglement, but also more importantly the structure of entanglement. We give an independent definition of a quantum wormhole as part of the proposal. This algebraic version of ER=EPR sheds light on a recent puzzle regarding spacetime disconnectivity in holographic systems with ${\cal O}(1/G_{N})$ entanglement. We discuss the emergence of quantum connectivity in the context of black hole evaporation and further argue that at the Page time, the black hole-radiation system undergoes a transition involving the transfer of an emergent type III$_{1}$ subalgebra of high complexity operators from the black hole to radiation. We argue this is a general phenomenon that occurs whenever there is an exchange of dominance between two competing quantum extremal surfaces.

  • Algebras, Regions, and Observers
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    In ordinary quantum field theory, one can define the algebra of observables in a given region in spacetime, but in the presence of gravity, it is expected that this notion ceases to be well-defined. A substitute that appears to make sense in the presence of gravity and that also is more operationally meaningful is to consider the algebra of observables along the timelike worldline of an observer. It is known that such an algebra can be defined in quantum field theory, and the timelike tube theorem of quantum field theory suggests that such an algebra is a good substitute for what in the absence of gravity is the algebra of a region. The static patch in de Sitter space is a concrete example in which it is useful to think in these terms and to explicitly incorporate an observer in the description.

  • Algorithmic Locality via Provable Convergence in Quantum Tensor Networks
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Belief propagation has recently emerged as a powerful framework for evaluating tensor networks in higher dimensions, combining computational efficiency with provable analytical guarantees. In this work, we develop the first end-to-end theory of tensor network belief propagation for a class of projected entangled pair states satisfying \emph{strong injectivity}. We show that when the injectivity parameter exceeds a constant threshold, BP fixed points can be found efficiently, and a cluster-corrected BP algorithm computes physical quantities to $1/\mathrm{poly}(N)$ error in $\mathrm{poly}(N)$ time for an $N$ qubit system. We identify a striking phenomenon we term \emph{algorithmic locality}: local perturbations of the tensor network affect the BP fixed point with an influence decaying rapidly with distance. As a result, updates to the fixed point after a local perturbation can be carried out using only local recomputation. Moreover, through the cluster expansion, this locality extends to observables, implying that local expectation values can be approximated from local data with controlled accuracy. Our results provide the first rigorous guarantee for the effectiveness of tensor-network belief propagation on a wide class of many-body states, bridging a gap between widely used numerical practice and provable algorithmic performance.

  • Almost-idempotent quantum channels and approximate $C^*$-algebras
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Let $\Phi$ be a unital completely positive (UCP) map on the space of operators on some Hilbert space. We assume that $\Phi$ is $\eta$-idempotent, namely, $\|\Phi^2-\Phi\|_{\mathrm{cb}} \le\eta$, and construct an associated $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra (of almost-invariant observables) for $\varepsilon=O(\eta)$. This type of structure has the axioms of a unital $C^*$ algebra but the associativity and other axioms involving the multiplication and the unit hold up to $\varepsilon$. We prove that any finite-dimensional $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra $A$ is $O(\varepsilon)$-isomorphic to some genuine $C^*$ algebra $B$. These bounds are universal, i.e. do not depend on the dimensionality or other parameters. When $A$ comes from a finite-dimensional $\eta$-idempotent UCP map $\Phi$, the $O(\eta)$-isomorphism and its inverse can be realized by UCP maps. This gives an approximate factorization of the quantum channel $\Phi^*$ into a decoding channel, producing a state on $B$, and an encoding channel.

  • An Instability of the Standard Model Creates the Anomalous Acceleration Without Dark Energy
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    We introduce a new asymptotic ansatz for spherical perturbations of the Standard Model of Cosmology (SM) which applies during the $p=0$ epoch, and prove that these perturbations trigger instabilities in the SM on the scale of the supernova data. These instabilities create a large, central region of uniform under-density which expands faster than the SM, and this central region of accelerated uniform expansion introduces into the SM {\it precisely} the same range of corrections to redshift vs luminosity as are produced by the cosmological constant in the theory of Dark Energy. A universal behavior is exhibited because all sufficiently small perturbations evolve to a single stable rest point. Moreover, we prove that these perturbations are consistent with, and the instability is triggered by, the one parameter family of self-similar waves which the authors previously proposed as possible time-asymptotic wave patterns for perturbations of the SM at the end of the radiation epoch. Using numerical simulations, we calculate the unique wave in the family that accounts for the same values of the Hubble constant and quadratic correction to redshift vs luminosity as in a universe with seventy percent Dark Energy, $\Omega_{\Lambda}\approx.7$. A numerical simulation of the third order correction associated with that unique wave establishes a testable prediction that distinguishes this theory from the theory of Dark Energy. This explanation for the anomalous acceleration, based on instabilities in the SM together with simple wave perturbations from the radiation epoch that trigger them, provides perhaps the simplest mathematical explanation for the anomalous acceleration of the galaxies that does not invoke Dark Energy.

  • An introductory review of the resource theory approach to thermodynamics
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    I give a self-contained introduction to the resource theory approach to quantum thermodynamics. I will introduce in an elementary manner the technical machinery necessary to unpack and prove the core statements of the theory. The topics covered include the so-called `many second laws of thermodynamics', thermo-majorisation and symmetry constraints on the evolution of quantum coherence. Among the elementary applications, I explicitly work out the bounds on deterministic work extraction and formation, discuss the complete solution of the theory for a single qubit and present the irreversibility of coherence transfers. The aim is to facilitate the task of those researchers interested in engaging and contributing to this topic, presenting scope and motivation of its core assumptions and discussing the relation between the resource theory and complementary approaches.

  • Assumptions of Physics - Home
    assumptionsofphysics.orgOther websites
    Summary

    A research program led by Christine Aidala and Gabriele Carcassi at the University of Michigan investigates the foundational assumptions underlying the basic laws of physics, specifically addressing why classical particles are defined by position and momentum while quantum systems are described by wave functions. Their approach aims to rigorously derive these laws from a small set of physical principles and assumptions, thereby clarifying the conditions under which each theory is valid and identifying potential failure points that could lead to new physics. By placing physical ideas at the center of the discussion rather than relegating them to after-the-fact interpretations, the program ensures that every mathematical symbol corresponds to a precise physical meaning, eliminating unphysical artifacts. This method fosters connections across diverse fields of science, mathematics, philosophy, and engineering, revealing recurring core concepts that span natural divisions. Ultimately, this formal framework allows researchers to pose deep questions regarding whether the requirements for deriving physical laws are statements about the actual world or merely conditions necessary for conducting science itself.

  • Atoms in molecules - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    The quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM), developed by Richard Bader, defines molecular structure based on the topology of electron density, identifying atoms as basins bounded by zero-flux surfaces and bonds as paths connecting stationary points. This approach treats atoms as proper open systems, allowing for the calculation of per-atom properties like kinetic energy and the satisfaction of a virial theorem. QTAIM has been applied to analyze phenomena such as unusually short intermolecular distances in molecular chlorine crystals, hydrogen-hydrogen interactions in phenanthrene and biphenyl, and the stabilization of kinked polycyclic benzenoids through specific bond paths that offset destabilizing factors. While the theory provides a physical basis for concepts like chemical bonding and offers unique quantum mechanical properties compared to other subsystem definitions, it faces criticism regarding the attribution of stability energy to these interactions, with some arguing that traditional resonance or steric explanations remain adequate.

  • Connecting afterglow light curves to the GRB central engine
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Gamma ray burst (GRB) afterglow light curves have the potential to inform us about presently unobserved stages in the aftermath of a neutron star merger. Using numerical simulations of short GRB afterglows we obtain an approximate quantitative connection between key aspects of the emission mechanism and the shapes of the resulting light curves. Employing simple, but efficient, parameterizations of the light curve based on a broken power law in terms of physical parameters, fitted to a large dataset of synthetic light curves, we apply basic machine learning techniques to determine the approximate connection between key input parameters of the forward shock model and the light curve parameters. Solving then the inverse problem, we find that the strength of the central engine can be reasonably accurately estimated even with very limited information. In particular, merely the position of jet-break in the on-axis, respectively the maximum in the off-axis light curve determines the kinetic energy at the tens of percent level.

  • Elasticity (physics) - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Continuum mechanics defines elasticity as a material's capacity to resist distortion and recover its original shape, contrasting this with plasticity where permanent deformation occurs. This behavior arises from atomic lattice changes in metals or polymer chain stretching in rubbers, often quantified by elastic moduli such as Young's modulus, which measure stress per unit strain. While Hooke's law describes a linear relationship between force and deformation for small strains in isotropic solids, most materials exhibit nonlinear stress-strain curves under larger deformations or require hyperelastic models derived from an energy potential function. Theoretical frameworks distinguish between Cauchy elasticity, hypoelasticity, and hyperelasticity, with engineering applications utilizing these principles to analyze structures while accounting for factors like porosity and cracks that reduce stiffness. Furthermore, thermodynamic perspectives classify materials as energy-elastic or entropy-elastic based on Helmholtz free energy, noting that microscopic factors like equilibrium molecular distances directly influence bulk modulus, though isolating temperature effects remains challenging due to dependencies on lattice form and molecular vibrations. A key limitation highlighted is that stiffness constants in Hooke's law are not strictly material properties but depend on the initial size and shape of the object, necessitating descriptions of behavior independent of geometry.

  • Entropic gravity - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Entropic gravity, proposed by Erik Verlinde in 2010, posits that gravity is an emergent force arising from quantum entanglement and the second law of thermodynamics rather than a fundamental interaction, offering an alternative explanation for dark matter and modified Newtonian dynamics. The theory successfully reproduces Einstein's field equations and explains galactic rotation curves in specific samples, deriving spacetime geometry from microscopic degrees of freedom. However, it faces significant challenges, including unnatural entropy assumptions for arbitrary potentials, failures to account for energy-momentum conservation in certain cosmological models, and potential violations of quantum coherence. Observational tests using galaxy lensing and dwarf galaxy rotation curves have yielded conflicting results, with some studies ruling out the theory unless additional dark matter components are included, while others find consistency. Critics also argue that the theory predicts rotation velocities far too low for massive galaxies full of gas clouds, creating a discrepancy that undermines its main success in predicting large galaxy rotation curves. Despite these limitations, the field continues to evolve with ongoing research into holographic principles and the thermodynamic aspects of gravity.

  • Experimental test of local observer-independence
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    The scientific method relies on facts, established through repeated measurements and agreed upon universally, independently of who observed them. In quantum mechanics, the objectivity of observations is not so clear, most dramatically exposed in Eugene Wigner's eponymous thought experiment where two observers can experience seemingly different realities. The question whether these realities can be reconciled in an observer-independent way has long remained inaccessible to empirical investigation, until recent no-go-theorems constructed an extended Wigner's friend scenario with four observers that allows us to put it to the test. In a state-of-the-art 6-photon experiment, we realise this extended Wigner's friend scenario, experimentally violating the associated Bell-type inequality by 5 standard deviations. If one holds fast to the assumptions of locality and free-choice, this result implies that quantum theory should be interpreted in an observer-dependent way.

  • Explicit Simplicial Discretization of Distributed-Parameter Port-Hamiltonian Systems
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    Simplicial Dirac structures as finite analogues of the canonical Stokes-Dirac structure, capturing the topological laws of the system, are defined on simplicial manifolds in terms of primal and dual cochains related by the coboundary operators. These finite-dimensional Dirac structures offer a framework for the formulation of standard input-output finite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems that emulate the behavior of distributed-parameter port-Hamiltonian systems. This paper elaborates on the matrix representations of simplicial Dirac structures and the resulting port-Hamiltonian systems on simplicial manifolds. Employing these representations, we consider the existence of structural invariants and demonstrate how they pertain to the energy shaping of port-Hamiltonian systems on simplicial manifolds.

  • Gibbs free energy - Wikipedia
    en.wikipedia.orgReference material
    Summary

    Gibbs free energy, a thermodynamic potential defined as G = H - TS, is the preferred term for quantifying the spontaneity of chemical reactions and the maximum non-pressure-volume work extractable from a closed system at constant temperature and pressure. Developed by Josiah Willard Gibbs in the 1870s, this concept replaced the earlier term "affinity" and serves as a necessary condition for reactions to proceed without external work input, where a negative change indicates a spontaneous process and equilibrium occurs when G is minimized. The framework extends to open systems through chemical potential terms and applies to both ideal and non-ideal systems, where fugacity accounts for deviations from ideal behavior. Historically, Gibbs introduced graphical methods using entropy, volume, and energy coordinates, later visualized by James Clerk Maxwell as a three-dimensional thermodynamic surface, establishing foundational concepts for understanding phase equilibria and chemical reactions. While the standard Gibbs free energy of formation quantifies energy changes during compound formation, modern usage increasingly omits the adjective "free." The fundamental equation for infinitesimal changes in Gibbs energy depends on heat, work, and entropy, with electrical work appearing in electrochemical cells via the Nernst equation, linking cell potential to the equilibrium constant and reaction quotient.

  • If the Universe Is a Hologram, This Long-Forgotten Math Could Decode It | Quanta Magazine
    www.quantamagazine.orgNews and articles
    Summary

    Recent research applies John von Neumann's 1930s theory of operator algebras to resolve limitations in earlier holographic models like AdS/CFT regarding the emergence of smooth space-time from quantum entanglement. By classifying quantum systems into Type I, II, and III algebras based on their entropy and entanglement properties, researchers such as Hong Liu and Sam Leutheusser demonstrate that smooth space-time corresponds to Type III algebras, while mild quantum fluctuations transition the system to Type II algebras. This rigorous mathematical framework allows for the calculation of entropy changes as matter falls into black holes, providing strong evidence that black hole entropy reflects microscopic degrees of freedom arranged on a two-dimensional surface, thereby reinforcing the holographic principle. While this approach offers a robust method for simulating extreme gravitational environments and describing the transition from fluctuating fields to geometric reality, current limitations remain in answering specific questions about the interior of black hole singularities.

  • inhomogeneous cosmology in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    Inhomogeneous cosmology investigates solutions to Einstein's equations that reject the standard assumption of spatial homogeneity, proposing that cosmic acceleration and phenomena like the Hubble tension may arise from gravitational backreaction rather than dark energy. Proponents, including researchers associated with the Timescape model, argue that voids expand faster than overdense regions, potentially explaining observed data without exotic components, though this view faces significant criticism from others who maintain that large-scale inhomogeneities cannot account for acceleration or resolve tensions within standard models. While numerical simulations and topological analyses suggest backreaction can alter expansion rates and challenge the cosmological principle, the field remains limited by the infancy of fully relativistic simulation codes, sensitivity to gauge choices, and unresolved debates regarding averaging formalisms. Consequently, despite evidence that backreaction is a real phenomenon with potential observational relevance, it currently cannot quantitatively explain all observed data without dark energy, leaving the question of whether inhomogeneities significantly affect large-scale cosmology as an open and contested issue.

  • Lagrangian density in nLab
    ncatlab.orgReference material
    Summary

    The classical mechanical system's laws of motion are defined by an action principle where actual paths are locally extremal paths of the action functional. In the Lagrangian formalism, a system is characterized by its configuration space and a real-valued Lagrangian function \(L(q, \dot{q}, t)\) that determines motion via the Euler-Lagrange equations. For continuum systems satisfying locality, the Lagrangian is expressed as a local quantity known as the Lagrangian density. In field theory, defined on a spacetime manifold \(X\) with a field bundle \(E\), the local Lagrangian is a horizontal differential form of degree \(n\) on the jet bundle \(j_\infty E\). This local Lagrangian is the pullback of a form on the jet bundle along the jet prolongation map, resulting in a differential form-valued functional on the space of sections. The integral of this form over a compact manifold \(X\) constitutes the local action functional, which serves as the basis for prequantized Lagrangian correspondences in quantum field theory.

  • Light-Cone Structure of Propagation of Entanglement
    arxiv.orgResearch papersSource abstract
    Summary

    For a wide class of bipartite systems with localized couplings, we establish existence of an effective light-cone for propagation of entanglement. This result yields a hard lower bound on the time it takes, under ideal conditions (no loss, no decoherence), to transport entanglement to a distant location (say, a node of a graph-structured quantum network), or to maintain it there.

  • Modified Gravity Theories and Cosmological Implications | Cosmology and Extragalactic Astronomy | Astronomical Sciences | Physical sciences | Topics | Nature Index
    www.nature.comResearch papers
    Summary

    Modified gravity theories extend Einstein's general relativity by introducing additional fields or geometric degrees of freedom, such as scalar, vector, or tensor components, to address cosmological puzzles like accelerated expansion and dark matter. Key frameworks include f(R) gravity, scalar-tensor theories, teleparallel approaches based on torsion or non-metricity, and massive gravity models assigning a finite mass to the graviton. These models predict modified expansion histories, novel screening mechanisms that restore general relativity in high-density environments, and distinctive imprints on gravitational lensing and cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Recent multi-probe surveys have placed stringent bounds on these modifications; for instance, combined weak lensing and redshift-space distortion measurements ruled out broad classes of f(R) models at the 5% level in the linear regime, while standard siren data from neutron-star mergers constrained graviton mass to show no significant deviation from massless propagation.

  • Neutron Transmutation Doping of Silicon – MIT Nuclear Reactor Laboratory
    nrl.mit.eduAcademic resources
    Summary

    The MIT-NRL Silicon Program irradiates high-purity silicon at the MIT Research Reactor (MITR-II) using Neutron Transmutation Doping (NTD) to manufacture microcircuits. The process utilizes the 4TH1-3 and 6TH1-2 horizontal through ports, which are tangent to the D2O Reflector Tank, to accommodate single crystal silicon ranging from 4 to 6 inches in diameter. During irradiation, thermal neutrons are captured by 30Si atoms (3% abundance), causing transmutation into 31Si which subsequently decays into 31P via beta emission, thereby creating free electrons and lowering resistivity. Crystals are loaded into 400 mm magnesium cans, transferred through an airlock, and pushed through the ports at speeds determined by reactor power and target resistivity. After irradiation, ingots undergo cleaning, radiation surveying, and quality control inspection before packaging and shipment to customers for use in transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits.

    In a restricted untwisted sector, Diaconescu, Moore & Witten [DMW00; DMW03] gave a quantum M-theoretic consistency check, at the level of partition functions, of what one may call Hypothesis K—that type IIA fluxes are quantized in K-theory. We show that the more recently discussed Hypothesis H—that 11D supergravity flux is quantized in coHomotopy—together with a topological smallness condition on the M-theory circle, systematically implies that IIA fluxes are quantized in a nonabelian refinement of twisted K-theory that reflects the previously neglected non-linear H7-flux Gauss law. This is a derivation of twisted K-theory from IR-completed 11D SuGra, and conversely a further consistency check on Hypothesis H from Hypothesis K. Here we briefly motivate and precisely state this result and some structural implica- tions; proofs are relegated to a comprehensive algebro-topological companion article.
